    ("integrate", "# Build a client on the dal protocol

A dal client talks to the agent over the dal protocol. Each message is one JSON object on one line. `dalgon` offers several ways in. This page builds a GUI client over `dalgon rpc`, then connects an editor and a Codex client.

Use the protocol to put your own UI, editor, or script in front of dal. The [protocol reference](protocol.md) lists every method.

## Choose a way in

| way in | command | frames |
|---|---|---|
| dal JSON-RPC on standard input and output | `dalgon rpc` | one JSON object per line |
| dal JSON-RPC on a local socket | `dalgon rpc --socket [FILE]` | one JSON object per line; `FILE` defaults to the per-user socket |
| Agent Client Protocol, for editors | `dalgon acp` | one JSON-RPC message per line |
| Codex app-server protocol | `dalgon app-server` | one message per line; frames omit `jsonrpc` |
| HTTP router, A2A, and WebSockets | `dalgon serve` | see [Run the dalgon model router and A2A server](serve.md) |

## Try it

Send one `initialize` request to `dalgon rpc`. The server ends when standard input ends.

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}' | dalgon rpc
```

The server answers with one line. Its `id` is `1`, and `result.protocolVersion` is `1`.

## Build a GUI client

Do these steps in order. Each request is one line on the standard input of `dalgon rpc`. Each reply is one line on its standard output.

1. Spawn `dalgon rpc`. Write one JSON object per line. Read one JSON object per line.
2. Send `initialize` first. List the capabilities you need. The result carries `protocolVersion`, the capabilities the server grants, and your `clientId`. Any other request before `initialize` fails with code `-32006` and `initialize must be the first request`. A second `initialize` fails with `-32600` and `initialize was already called`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":1,"clientInfo":{"name":"my-gui","version":"0.1.0"},"capabilities":["sessions","approval"]}}
   ```

3. Call `session/list` to show past sessions. `limit` runs from 1 to 500. A page that has more rows carries `nextCursor`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"session/list","params":{"limit":10}}
   ```

4. Call `session/open` to start or resume one. `workspace` must be an absolute path. The result carries `sessionId`, `gen`, and `view`. Other `ref` types are `resume` with `key` and `workspace`, `continue` with `workspace`, and `ephemeral` with `workspace`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"session/open","params":{"ref":{"type":"new","workspace":"/home/me/project"}}}
   ```

5. Call `session/subscribe` to receive updates. The reply holds `gen` and `seq`. Then the server sends `session/update` notifications. Each one names its update type in `params.update.type`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"session/subscribe","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>"}}
   ```

6. Call `session/submit` with a `prompt` command to start a turn.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"session/submit","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>","command":{"type":"prompt","expect":"idle","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Explain src/main.rs"}]}}}
   ```

7. Render updates as they arrive. A `request_opened` update asks you for an answer. Answer it once with `session/answer`. Use the request `id` as `requestId`. The `answer` is `{"type":"approve"}`, `{"type":"approve_for_session"}`, `{"type":"decline"}`, `{"type":"cancel"}`, or `{"type":"value","value":...}`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"session/answer","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>","requestId":"<requestId>","answer":{"type":"approve"}}}
   ```

8. Cancel a running turn with `session/submit` and a `cancel` command. `turn` is the number of the running turn.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"session/submit","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>","command":{"type":"cancel","scope":{"type":"turn","turn":1}}}}
   ```

9. Read a stored blob with `blob/read`. Pass `sessionId` and `blobId`.
10. Reconnect with `session/subscribe`. Pass the `gen` you hold and `after`, the last `seq` you saw. A stale `gen` makes the server send a resync and resume at the head. An `after` beyond the head fails with `invalid params for session/subscribe: after <n> is beyond seq <m>`.
11. Generate your types from `protocol/schema`.

A wrong parameter fails with code `-32602`. The message reads `invalid params for <method>: <detail>`. A relative workspace fails with `invalid params for session/open: workspace must be an absolute path`.

## Client rules

- R1: answer each request exactly once.
- R2: never invent missing updates. Resync on gaps.
- R3: cancel cleanly. Do not abandon turns.
- R4: keep tokens secret. Never log them.
- R5: use one adapter for each transport. Never stack one adapter on another.
- R6: validate server replies tolerantly. Ignore unknown fields.

## Connect an editor over ACP

An editor that speaks the Agent Client Protocol starts `dalgon acp` as a child process. Register `dalgon acp` as the agent command in the editor settings. The command reads one JSON-RPC message per line on standard input. It writes one per line on standard output.

Check the command by hand:

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}' | dalgon acp
```

The reply carries `id` `1` and a `result`.

## Connect a Codex client

`dalgon app-server` serves the Codex app-server protocol. Its frames omit the `jsonrpc` member. A second `initialize` fails with code `-32600`.

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"clientInfo":{"name":"gate-client","title":"gate-client","version":"0.1.0"},"capabilities":{}}}' | dalgon app-server
```

The reply carries `id` `1` and a `result`.

## Next

- [Protocol](protocol.md) lists every method, capability, and error code.
- [Embed dal in a Rust program](sdk.md) shows the same agent as a Rust library.
- [Run the dalgon model router and A2A server](serve.md) serves the protocol over WebSockets.

    ("models", "# Providers, models, and thinking levels

Supported configuration API families: `openai_chat`, `openai_responses`, `openai_codex`, `anthropic`, `bedrock`, `cursor`, `devin`, `droid`, `gitlab`, `google-generative-ai`, `google-vertex`, `google-gemini-cli`, `google-antigravity`, `mistral`, `ollama`, and `pi-messages`. Built-in provider sign-in supports OpenAI, OpenAI Codex, Anthropic, Factory Droid, GitLab Duo, GitHub Copilot, Radius, OpenRouter, Cursor, and Devin, alongside configured providers and API-key presets. Run `dalgon login`, then pick a model.

Sign-in flows vary by provider:
- OpenAI Codex authenticates through browser OAuth with a local callback, with fallback to device authorization.
- Anthropic and GitLab Duo authenticate through browser OAuth with a local callback or code paste; GitLab Duo also supports personal access tokens via `GITLAB_TOKEN`.
- Factory Droid authenticates through WorkOS device-code sign-in (`dalgon login factory-droid`), which displays the verification URL and user code and polls for completion without binding a local callback port.
- GitHub Copilot authenticates through GitHub device authorization (`dalgon login github-copilot`), prompting for an optional GitHub Enterprise URL or domain (blank for `github.com`), displaying the verification URL and user code, and polling for completion without binding a local callback port. Copilot also accepts a token via `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN` or `dalgon login github-copilot --api-key`. Stored credentials are saved to `auth.json` as a raw token or a structured envelope with the token, enterprise domain, and discovered account endpoint. The sign-in epilogue applies best-effort model policy enablement directly without querying the model catalog at sign-in time.
- Radius supports browser OAuth discovery and loopback callback (`dalgon login radius`) or RFC 8628 device authorization (`dalgon login radius --device-auth`), while retaining API-key sign-in.
- OpenRouter supports browser PKCE sign-in (`dalgon login openrouter`) and stores the returned durable key as an API-key credential, while retaining API-key sign-in.
- Cursor supports the Cursor CLI browser sign-in (`dalgon login cursor`): dalgon prints the Cursor login page, you approve it in the browser, and dalgon polls Cursor until it releases the tokens. No local callback port is bound and nothing is pasted. After sign-in, dalgon fetches the models your account can use; a failed fetch keeps the sign-in. The stored OAuth credential refreshes automatically; when Cursor ends the session, run `dalgon login cursor` again.
- Devin supports the Devin CLI browser sign-in (`dalgon login devin`) with a local callback on `127.0.0.1:59653` or a pasted code; when that port is busy, paste the code shown in the browser. The returned long-lived token is stored as an OAuth credential that is never refreshed; when it expires, run `dalgon login devin` again.

Ollama (`ollama`) and Ollama Cloud (`ollama-cloud`) speak Ollama's native `/api/chat` NDJSON wire (`api = "ollama"`), not its OpenAI-compatible `/v1` surface. `ollama` defaults to `http://127.0.0.1:11434` and reads `OLLAMA_API_KEY`; a local server takes no key, so set `providers.ollama.auth = "none"`. `ollama-cloud` defaults to `https://ollama.com` and takes its key from `OLLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY` or `dalgon login ollama-cloud --api-key`. The model list comes from `/api/tags`, and every listed model is probed once with `/api/show`, six at a time, for what it supports: a `thinking` capability opens the reasoning levels (GPT-OSS `low` to `high`, DeepSeek V4 `low`, `high`, `max`, any other self-hosted model `low` to `max`), `vision` opens image input, a model without `tools` is sent none, and the `<architecture>.context_length` member sets the context window. A failed probe keeps the model's row from the last good refresh, and a server with no `/api/show` still lists its models. On Ollama Cloud, `num_predict` never exceeds 65,536, DeepSeek V4 Pro and Flash carry that cap as their output limit, and replayed history leaves out assistant reasoning (GLM 5.2 excepts it); a self-hosted server takes any limit and replays reasoning.

Mistral (`mistral`, `api = "mistral"`) takes `MISTRAL_API_KEY` as a bearer token and speaks the native conversations wire: `POST <base>/conversations` with typed `inputs` entries, `instructions`, `completion_args`, and `store: false`, never Chat Completions. A model whose card says `capabilities.reasoning` accepts `reasoning_effort` `none` and `high` (`zai-glm-5-2`: `none`, `high`, `max`; `zai-glm-5-3`: `low`, `high`, `max`); any other model, and any model id with no card, is sent no reasoning control. Prior reasoning replays as `thinking` chunks only while reasoning is on. When a reasoning run carries a signed chunk (a `thinking` chunk with a non-empty `signature`, the optional nullable string the Conversations schema documents for replaying reasoning across turns), dal keeps the run's chunks verbatim, in arrival order, and replays the full array ahead of the message text on the next turn; a run without a signature emits no replay record and journals as before. As dal policy, not a Mistral mandate, verbatim replay applies only to an assistant message this family and model produced, only while reasoning is on, and only when the stored array still has the recorded shape and text; anything else, including every message from another family or model, replays as one text-only `thinking` chunk.

Radius (`radius`, `api = "pi-messages"`) takes an API key from `RADIUS_API_KEY` or `dalgon login radius --api-key`, sent as a bearer token to `https://radius.pi.dev/v1/messages`. Its browser flow discovers the gateway authorization endpoint and uses a loopback callback; `dalgon login radius --device-auth` uses RFC 8628 device authorization. The model list comes from the gateway's `/v1/config` document, cached like every other provider list. Any backend that speaks the pi-messages wire can be configured with `api = "pi-messages"` and a `base_url` that ends at the path before `/messages`.

OpenRouter (`openrouter`, `api = "openai_responses"`) supports browser PKCE sign-in with `dalgon login openrouter` and stores the returned durable key as an API-key credential. It also accepts `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` or `dalgon login openrouter --api-key`.

Cursor (`cursor`, `api = "cursor"`) defaults to `https://api2.cursor.sh`. Besides the browser sign-in it accepts an access token from `CURSOR_ACCESS_TOKEN` (or its `CURSOR_API_KEY` alias) or `dalgon login cursor --api-key`, sent as a bearer token.

Devin (`devin`, `api = "devin"`) defaults to the Cascade endpoint `https://server.codeium.com`. Besides the browser sign-in it accepts `DEVIN_API_KEY` or `dalgon login devin --api-key`. The sign-in host `api.devin.ai` only issues the token; requests always go to the Cascade endpoint.

Bedrock providers authenticate using captured AWS credential sources (environment variables, shared configuration and credential files, SSO, external credential processes, or IAM roles) or a stored bearer token in `auth.json`. Bedrock does not provide an interactive sign-in flow. `dalgon login status` evaluates readiness across effective configured provider families and aliases, reporting `ready` when an AWS credential source or stored bearer token is present, or `not configured` when missing.

Use this page to connect a provider, choose a default model, and set a thinking level.

Azure OpenAI rides on the `openai_chat` and `openai_responses` families: shape a provider entry as Azure (see [Settings in dal.toml](config.md#azure-openai)) and pick a provider-qualified model such as `openai/gpt-5.4`. The catalog id maps to its Azure deployment through the entry's `deployments` table, falling back to the id itself. Requests carry the key in an `api-key` header rather than as a bearer token.

Stored credentials live in `auth.json` at mode 0600 without secret echoing, saving raw API keys, OAuth tokens, or structured envelopes.

## Sign in

Run the sign-in command in a terminal. It lists the providers you can sign in to. Type the number or the id of one provider.

```sh
dalgon login
```

To sign in without a prompt, name the provider. Pipe the key on standard input:

```sh
printf %s "$KEY" | dalgon login anthropic --api-key
```

```text
Saved Anthropic credentials. Run dal to pick a model.
```

`--api-key` reads the key from standard input. `--device-auth` uses the provider's device flow, where the provider offers one. A provider also counts as signed in when its key variable is set. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and `OPENAI_API_KEY` are two of them.

The `openai-codex` provider signs in with a ChatGPT account. It takes no API key. Passing `--api-key` fails with `dalgon: openai-codex uses ChatGPT sign-in: API keys are not accepted`. Run `dalgon login openai-codex`, or use an OpenAI API key with `dalgon login openai --api-key`.

Check the result. The command prints one row per provider and exits 0 when at least one provider is ready:

```text
anthropic      ready           api_key
openai         not configured
```

Sign out with `dalgon logout [PROVIDER]`. Without a provider, it removes every stored credential.

## Pick a model

List the models. The table shows built-in prices and their source. Pass a pattern to filter the list, or `--json` for JSON.

```sh
dalgon models
dalgon models claude
```

If the list fails, check the network and sign in again with `dalgon login PROVIDER`.

Run `dal` once and pick a model from the list. Dal saves the choice. In a session, type `/model [provider/model]` to switch and `/login` to sign in.

A model id has the form `<family>/<model>`, such as `anthropic/claude-sonnet-5` or `openai-codex/gpt-5.6-luna`. These families are spelled `openai-chat`, `openai-responses`, `openai-codex`, and `anthropic`. To set a default by hand, write it in `dal.toml`. An alias gives a long id a short name:

```toml
model = "fast"
thinking = "high"

[aliases]
fast = "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5"
```

For one run, pass the model and the level on the command line:

```sh
dalgon -m anthropic/claude-sonnet-5 --thinking high -p "Summarize the staged diff"
```

With no model set, dal stops with `dalgon: no model is configured: dal.toml has no model key and --model was not given`. The fix line reads `Run dalgon once and pick a model after sign-in, or pass --model ID. See dalgon models.`

For another endpoint, add a `[providers.<name>]` table. It needs `api` and `base_url`, and `key_env` for the variable that holds the key. [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) lists the `model`, `thinking`, `aliases`, and `providers` keys.

## Set the thinking level

Seven levels exist. The default is `medium`.

| level | meaning |
|---|---|
| `off` | no reasoning |
| `minimal` | minimal reasoning |
| `low` | low reasoning |
| `medium` | medium reasoning |
| `high` | high reasoning |
| `xhigh` | extra-high reasoning |
| `max` | the most reasoning the model supports |

Set the level with `thinking` in `dal.toml`, `--thinking LEVEL` for one run, or `/thinking [level]` in a session. Each API takes the level in its own form. Dal maps the level for each API and clamps it to the limits of the model.

Dal sends a temperature only when the model allows one and the thinking level is `off`. At any other level, dal drops the temperature.

## Know what the providers send

- Once a response has delivered output, no failure retries and no sign-in refresh runs. A transport cut before delivery retries with backoff. The longest single wait is 60 seconds.
- Codex requests send the header `originator: dalgon`.
- A Claude OAuth sign-in adds Claude Code markers to each request. They include the beta headers, the user agent, an `x-app: web` header, and an identity line at the start of the system prompt. API keys and bearer keys never send them.
- Luna Reserve is an opt-in Codex model with the id `gpt-reserve`. It opens only when the included usage of your ChatGPT plan runs out. Then dal prints `note: usage is blocked. Luna Reserve is available: type /model gpt-reserve to switch.` It is never a default model. On an account without it, dal says `Luna Reserve is not available for this account`, and the fix is to switch to another model.

## Next

- [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) lists every config key.
- [Slash commands](commands.md) lists `/model`, `/thinking`, and `/login`.
- [Run the dalgon model router and A2A server](serve.md) serves these models over HTTP.
## Usage, cost, and premium requests

Each turn records token counts and, when the provider reports them, a USD cost and a premium request count. A reported provider cost always wins; otherwise dal computes cost from the resolved price table (configured `prices` entry, then live catalog, then compiled snapshot). Computed cost is `(uncached input × input rate) + (cached input × cached_input rate) + (cache writes × cache_write or input rate) + (output × output rate) + (reasoning × reasoning rate)` per million tokens, with tier overrides applied by request size. `premium_requests` counts provider metered requests: an absent value means unknown for that turn, while `0` means the provider measured zero. Session cost displays stay `unknown` when neither a reported cost nor a resolvable price exists.

    ("philosophy", "# Philosophy: why dal has one extension door

dal is a small coding agent with one door. Everything that extends it comes in through that door: plugins, other programs, every way in, and dalgona's batteries. The primary binary is `dalgon`, with `dal` and `dl` as aliases.

## Why dal

dal has no private inside. Its own batteries register through the plugin interface. dal alone is a complete agent. dalgona adds opinions. Both load the same plugins. The [requirements](requirements.md) page lists what dal and dalgona must meet.

## One door

The door is one public interface that plugins, programs, and clients share. In process, the Rust interface of the Host and Agent seam carries five operations. They are one snapshot, one change stream, one command path, one request and answer pair, and one blob read. In plain words, a client reads the session state, follows its updates, sends a command, answers a request from the agent, and fetches stored data. A `Host` owns the live sessions. An `Agent` is a handle to one session. The TUI uses these and nothing else. Across processes, a JSON-RPC protocol carries the same operations. `dalgon rpc` serves it over stdio or a local socket. Every message has a JSON Schema. `docs/read` serves both manuals.

## Plugins in Starlark

A plugin is a directory with one `plugin.star` in the data root. A plugin publishes one `plugin` value. The value registers tools, commands, hooks, skills, rules, and prompt text. It also declares the operations each tool and hook may request. Every effect still needs your approval. Nine lifecycle events exist. Each has a declared result type. A Rust extension sees a tenth. Questions travel as data to whichever way in you use. Load has no compile step. A broken plugin stops startup and names `path:line:col`. `/reload` evaluates the plugins again and prints counts (for example `Reloaded 2 plugins: 3 tools. New turns use them. A running turn keeps the plugins it started with.`). On failure, it prints `reload failed: <rendered error>` and `the previous plugin set stays live`. A plugin that loads in dalgon loads in dalgona. A plugin runs with your permissions, so read it before you install it. To bring over a pi extension, follow [Port a pi extension to a dal plugin](convert-pi.md).

## Models

Four API families exist. Run `dalgon login`. Then pick a model. `/model` changes the model in a session. `/thinking` changes the thinking level in a session. See [Providers, models, and thinking levels](models.md).

## History you can trust

Each session is a journal. A record counts as saved only after dal syncs it to disk. A session is a tree. `-c` continues a session. `-r` resumes a session. `/export` writes a file you can share yourself. See [Sessions, history, and compaction](sessions.md).

## Context you control

dal builds the system prompt from parts you control (skills, rules, plugin sections). `AGENTS.md` files and `SYSTEM.md` do not reach the model. `dal://prompt` lists the parts that reach the model. See [The system prompt](prompt.md). Compaction starts by default at 85 percent of the context window. Long, stable text can go out as an image. The exact text stays readable at `letter://<id>`.

## Tools and approval

Every mode lists `read`, `search`, `patch`, `exec`, and `eval`. The eval-first and eval-only modes also reach plugin tools and prompt sections marked `eval_only`. [Tools, modes, and approval](tools.md) explains each mode. A call you deny outside `eval` stays denied inside it. `eval` is not a sandbox. `patch` supports several edit styles. One setting picks the style, and the style follows the model. By default dal asks before every `patch` and every `exec`. `--approval ask|edits|all` sets the approval ladder. When no person can answer, dal denies the call and says why. An optional sandbox, off by default, guards the home directory. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

## Steer or follow up

You can type while dal works. A steer reaches the model at the next safe point. A follow-up waits for the turn to end. Stop ends the turn at once. See [Terminal interface](terminal.md) for the keys.

## Many ways in, one protocol

| Way in | Start |
|---|---|
| Terminal (inline) | `dal` |
| Terminal (fullscreen) | `dal` with fullscreen screen |
| Print | `dalgon` print flags |
| JSON | `dalgon` JSON flags |
| ACP | editor ACP adapter |
| RPC | `dalgon rpc` |
| Router | `dalgon serve` |
| A2A | `dalgon serve --a2a` |

`dalgon serve` listens on your machine only unless you add `--public`, which requires a token. See [Router and A2A](serve.md). No desktop, web, or mobile app ships. Any such app is a client of the protocol, not a fork. See [Build a client on the dal protocol](integrate.md).

## Built for large runs

The stress gate exercises 501 child sessions and 201 shell jobs with scripted models. On the idle-machine timing lane (`DAL_TIMING_BUDGETS`), it requires RSS below 256 MiB, fewer than 4096 open handles, and cancellation P99 below 250 ms. These are gate limits, not promises about your machine.

## Text in every language

dal measures text the way your terminal draws it. The cursor, wrapping, and cuts never split a character.

## The manual is inside

dal documents itself at `dal://`. dalgona adds `dalgona://`. The model reads pages with `read`. You read them with `dalgon docs`.

## dalgona

dalgona is dal with batteries. dalgona enables every built-in battery by default through dal's same public extension door. The built-in batteries are orchestration, history, quality, judged, web, work, MCP, review, ask, skills, and ttsr-rules. By default, dalgona enables symbol search, AST edit, the `hashline` edit style, and the complexity guard. It also provides plan and todo, rich ask, web search and fetch, an MCP client, and a review loop. It keeps its own configuration, data, and sessions. This repository uses one root Cargo workspace and one root `Cargo.lock` to resolve dalgona's dal dependencies locally. Releases publish dal and dalgona separately. dal and dalgona are distributed under the Sustainable Use License. The licensor is `metaphorics`.

## What we did not build

dal has no MCP client. dalgona ships one. A plugin can reach HTTP services with the `net.fetch` operation. dal does not load plugins from the workspace. dal has no sandbox by default and no network restriction. dal has no plan or todo. dalgona ships both. dal has no subagents by default. The `agents` operations are one door away. Neither dal nor dalgona has LSP. Search plus AST edit is the surface. dal never uploads. `/export` writes a file you can share yourself. dal has no self-rebuild. `/reload` reloads plugins. `eval` accepts nothing but Starlark. dal has no second store. The journal is the only store. The binary has no browser front end.

## Next

- [Quickstart](quickstart.md): sign in and run your first turn.
- [Plugins](plugins.md): add a tool or command through the door.
- [Protocol](protocol.md): build a client on the same operations.

    ("plugins", "# Plugins: tools, commands, hooks, skills, and rules

A plugin is Starlark that adds tools, slash commands, hooks, skills, rules, and prompt text to dal. It is one directory holding one file, `plugin.star`. That file publishes one value named `plugin`. Nothing else registers. A tool you build but do not attach to `plugin` does not exist. A plugin runs with your permissions, so read it before you install it.

## Write a first plugin

You write one file, turn it on, grant it one permission, and call it. The plugin finds `TODO` comments in your code.

Make a directory under the data root and write `plugin.star` into it. The directory name is the plugin name.

```sh
d="${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/dal/plugins/quality"
mkdir -p "$d"
cat > "$d/plugin.star" <<'EOF'
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def find_todos(ctx, args):
    page = ctx.tools.search("TODO", path = args.path)
    return {
        "matches": [
            {"path": hit.path, "line": hit.line, "text": hit.text}
            for hit in page.matches[:args.limit]
        ],
        "truncated": page.truncated or len(page.matches) > args.limit,
    }

todos = dal.tool(
    description = "Find TODO comments under a path.",
    input = dal.schema(
        path = dal.string(default = "."),
        limit = dal.integer(default = 20, min = 1, max = 200),
    ),
    uses = ["tools.search"],
    run = find_todos,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "quality",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"todos": todos},
    commands = {
        "todos": dal.command(tool = todos, positional = ["path"]),
    },
)
EOF
```

On Windows, make the directory with the PowerShell command in [Config and data roots](install.md#config-and-data-roots). Then save the same Starlark text as `plugin.star` in it.

Turn it on. Add its name to the `plugins` key in `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/dal/dal.toml`. Put the key above any `[table]` header. Create the file if it does not exist.

```toml
plugins = ["quality"]
```

Check that dal loads the plugin. A load error stops the command and names `path:line:col`.

```sh
dalgon plugin list
```

The handler calls `tools.search`, which reads files. So the plugin asks for the `fs.read` service. No grant exists yet:

```text
quality (user): services: fs.read; persistent grant: not granted
```

Grant the service. Run the command from the workspace where you will use the plugin.

```sh
dalgon plugin grant quality
```

```text
Granted "quality" (user): fs.read.
```

Run `dalgon plugin list` again. The row now ends with `persistent grant: granted`. A grant covers one workspace and one version of the plugin code. When you edit `plugin.star`, grant again.

Skip the grant, and dal asks on the first call in the terminal. A headless run cannot ask, so dal denies the call. The denial reads `denied: plugin "quality" has no grant for the "fs.read" service; approve the plugin's grant request when it asks, then try again`.

Run dal. The model can now call the tool. You can type `/quality:todos src`. The result holds `matches`, a list of records with `path`, `line`, and `text`, and a `truncated` flag.

Four things carry the whole design:

- `load("@dal/v1", "dal")` appears once. It is the only import a plugin may use.
- A handler is `run(ctx, args)`. dal checks the arguments against `input` and fills defaults. Only then does it call the handler.
- `uses` lists every operation the handler may request. dal denies a call to any other operation and ends the handler.
- `plugin` is the only value a plugin publishes. Its `name` must equal the directory name.

## Fill in the plugin value

`dal.plugin` takes keywords only. `name` and `version` are required.

| keyword | value | default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | the directory name: lowercase letters, digits, `_`, `-`, starting with a letter, at most 64 characters | required |
| `version` | a SemVer string such as `"0.1.0"` | required |
| `config` | a `dal.schema` for the plugin's settings | none |
| `state_version` | a positive integer naming the shape of saved state | `1` |
| `tools` | a map from a local key to a `dal.tool` | empty |
| `commands` | a map from a key to a `dal.command` | empty |
| `hooks` | a list of `dal.on` | empty |
| `skills` | a map from a name to a `dal.skill` | empty |
| `rules` | a map from a name to a `dal.rule` | empty |
| `prompt` | one static prompt section, or `None` | `None` |
| `models` | a map from a local key to a `dal.model` | empty |

A tool key `todos` in plugin `quality` has the identity `quality.todos`. One `dal.tool` can have at most one key. A tool with no key still serves a command. dal keeps saved state apart for each plugin and each `state_version`. Changing the version does not migrate old state.

## Define a tool

`dal.tool` takes keywords only.

| keyword | meaning | default |
|---|---|---|
| `description` | what the model reads to choose the tool | required |
| `input` | a `dal.schema` for the arguments | required |
| `run` | the handler, `run(ctx, args)` | required |
| `uses` | the operations the handler may request | `[]` |
| `output` | a `dal.schema` the returned value must satisfy | none |
| `visibility` | `"model"`, `"deferred"`, or `"eval_only"` | `"model"` |

`"model"` puts the tool in the model's ordinary tool list. `"deferred"` keeps the tool out of the list until the model first calls it by name. The call runs at once. The tool joins the list in the next request and in every later request. A request offers exactly one way to find deferred tools. On first-party Anthropic models from Opus, Sonnet, Fable, and Mythos 4.5 on, Anthropic's own tool search finds them. Each tool travels in the request, marked `defer_loading`. Every other model gets the `tool_search` tool. It lists matches and changes nothing. A plugin tool named `tool_search` replaces both. `"eval_only"` reaches the tool only through `eval`.

### Describe arguments with a schema

`dal.schema(**fields)` builds the schema. Each field is one of these constructors. Keywords are named. The first argument of `enum`, `list`, `optional`, and `nullable` is positional.

| constructor | accepts |
|---|---|
| `dal.string` | `min_len`, `max_len`, `default` |
| `dal.integer` | `min`, `max`, `default` |
| `dal.number` | `min`, `max`, `default` |
| `dal.boolean` | `default` |
| `dal.enum(values)` | a list of strings, `default` |
| `dal.list(item)` | `min_len`, `max_len`; `item` is a bare type |
| `dal.optional(type)` | the caller may leave the field out |
| `dal.nullable(type)` | the field is required but may be `None` |

A field is required unless it has a `default` or you wrap it in `optional`. When a caller leaves out an `optional` field, the handler reads `dal.MISSING`:

```starlark
def note(ctx, args):
    if args.tag == dal.MISSING:
        return "No tag given."
    return "Tag: " + args.tag
```

Field names are plain identifiers and never start with `_`. Bounds must not contradict each other. dal coerces nothing. The string `"5"` does not satisfy an integer field. A truthy value does not satisfy a boolean.

### Return a result

Return plain data. That data is the result. Three helpers say more:

- `dal.ok(value)` returns a success explicitly.
- `dal.err(code, message, details)` returns a failure the model can read. `details` is optional. The codes `failed`, `exit_nonzero`, `unavailable`, `conflict`, `busy`, `cancelled`, `observation_unavailable`, `invocation_mismatch`, and `indeterminate` belong to dal. `dal.err` refuses them.
- `dal.output(value = ..., view = ...)` separates the data from its display. A view is `{"type": "text", "text": "..."}`, `{"type": "table", "columns": [...], "rows": [[...]]}`, an intact view from `tools.read`, or a list of views. Table rows hold scalar values. A view changes what people see, never the status of the call.

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def count(ctx, args):
    page = ctx.tools.search(args.pattern, path = args.path)
    total = len(page.matches)
    return dal.output(
        value = {"count": total, "truncated": page.truncated},
        view = {
            "type": "table",
            "columns": ["pattern", "matches"],
            "rows": [[args.pattern, total]],
        },
    )

def branch(ctx, args):
    result = ctx.try_call(ctx.tools.exec, "git branch --show-current")
    if not result.ok:
        return dal.err("no_git", "Could not read the branch: " + result.error.message)
    return dal.ok(result.value)

count_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Count matches for a pattern.",
    input = dal.schema(
        pattern = dal.string(min_len = 1),
        path = dal.string(default = "."),
    ),
    uses = ["tools.search"],
    run = count,
)

branch_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Show the current git branch.",
    input = dal.schema(),
    uses = ["tools.exec"],
    run = branch,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "report",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"count": count_tool, "branch": branch_tool},
)
```

A plain dictionary that happens to contain `ok = False` is still data. Only `dal.err` reports a failure.

## Reach the outside with ctx

`ctx.config` holds the validated settings. Every other field of `ctx` is a group of operations. Each call returns its value directly:

```starlark
view = ctx.tools.read("src/lib.rs")
```

`tools.read` returns a view with `path`, `header`, `truncated`, and `rows`. Each row has `line`, `text`, and `complete`. `tools.search` returns a page with `matches` and `truncated`. Each match has `path`, `line`, `text`, and a `source` read view. A handler cannot return a view itself. Return plain data. To display the view, pass it as the `view` of `dal.output`.

An operation that fails stops the handler with the error. To handle an expected failure yourself, pass the operation, not its result, to `ctx.try_call`. You get a result with `ok`, `value`, and `error`. `unwrap()` returns the value or raises the failure again. Denial, cancellation, and hard limits still stop the handler. `try_call` cannot catch them and never retries.

These are the operations. A handler may call only those in its `uses`.

| group | operations | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `tools` | `read`, `search`, `patch`, `exec` | read files, search, edit files, run a command |
| `models` | `infer` | ask a model for a completion |
| `net` | `fetch` | make an HTTP request to an allowed destination |
| `ask` | `confirm`, `select`, `text` | ask the user a question |
| `state` | `read`, `write`, `delete` | keep data for this plugin and session |
| `agents` | `start`, `wait`, `cancel`, `list` | run child sessions |
| `jobs` | `start`, `wait`, `cancel`, `list`, `text` | run background jobs |
| `turn` | `cancel`, `steer`, `wake`, `is_idle` | steer the running turn or start one |
| `env` | `read` | read an allowed environment variable |
| `mcp` | `call` | call an MCP tool when a client is present |

Write the id as `group.operation`, for example `"state.write"`. Ids are exact. Use no wildcards and no duplicates. Use at most 64 ids per declaration. The positional argument of `tools.read` is `path`. The positional argument of `tools.search` is `pattern`. The positional argument of `tools.exec` is `command`. Every other argument is named. Call `ctx.describe("tools.exec")` to see the keywords of one operation.

`agents.start` does not accept a per-call `tools` list. If you pass one, the call fails with an argument error. If you omit `name`, the call starts an unnamed child. A given `name` must be unique among the sessions in the workspace. A taken name refuses the start. When policy or input stops a child, `agents.start` answers `refused` with a typed `reason`. The reasons are `max_depth` (`child sessions cannot start children here: agents.max_depth = <n>.`), `workspace_unresolved`, `workspace_outside_root`, and `model_unroutable`. Show the reason text to the user. A `cancelled` reply still means the child was cancelled.

`uses` asks. It does not grant. Each effect still needs a live grant and passes the approval ladder, so `tools.patch` and `tools.exec` ask before they run. `ask` operations must be in `uses` but need no grant. `turn.wake` refuses after 20 turns in a row that wake started with no user prompt. `models.forward` exists only for model handlers. Plugins cannot use it.

State is explicit and session-scoped. A read returns a record with `present`, `value` (when present), and `revision`. A write or delete must pass the `revision` from a read as `expected`. A stale revision fails with `conflict`. `ctx.try_call` can catch that. Keys match `[a-z][a-z0-9_.-]{0,63}`. An ephemeral session returns `unavailable` for state. The `todo` example keeps a list this way. Read it at `dal://examples/todo`.

A handler cannot call another plugin's tool. One plugin can share code between its handlers with plain functions, and two plugins can read the same file.

## Add a command

`dal.command(tool = ..., positional = [...], description = ...)` binds a slash command to a tool. The command runs that tool once, with the same schema and defaults a model call gets. Without `description`, the tool's description is the command's summary. The command name is `/<plugin>:<key>`. The key uses lowercase letters, digits, `_`, and `-`. It starts with a letter and has at most 64 characters. A name that clashes with a built-in command is an error that names both claimants.

`positional` lists scalar fields in order. A required field cannot follow an optional one. The rest take `--field=value`. For strings, `--field value` also works. Booleans take `--field` and `--no-field`. Lists and records take one JSON value: `--field=JSON`. `--` ends option parsing. Single and double quotes group a token. A backslash escapes the next character outside single quotes. Assigning one field twice is an error. Nothing expands. There are no globs, variables, or shell.

## Hook into the turn

`dal.on(event, run, uses = [...])` runs `run(ctx, event)` at one lifecycle event. The event value carries its payload as attributes, such as `event.tool`, and the methods that return a verdict.

| event | payload | the handler returns | may request |
|---|---|---|---|
| `session_start` | `session`, `workspace`, `resumed` | `None` | `state.read`, `state.write`, `state.delete` |
| `session_end` | `session`, `reason` | `None` | `state.read`, `state.write`, `state.delete` |
| `input` | `text` | `event.continue_()`, `event.transform(text)`, `event.handled()` | nothing |
| `before_turn` | `turn`, `text` | `event.continue_()`, `event.append(text)` | nothing |
| `before_request` | `turn`, `round`, `model`, `caps`, `params` | `event.continue_()`, `event.params(...)` | nothing |
| `tool_call` | `turn`, `call`, `tool`, `args` | `event.allow()`, `event.block(reason)`, `event.rewrite(args)` | nothing |
| `tool_result` | `turn`, `call`, `tool`, `ok`, `preview` | `None` | `state.read`, `state.write`, `state.delete` |
| `turn_end` | `turn`, `stop` | `None` | `state.read`, `state.write`, `state.delete` |
| `settled` | `turn` | `None` | `state.read` |

The four hooks that decide something (`input`, `before_turn`, `before_request`, `tool_call`) are pure. They see only the event, the plugin's config, and fixed metadata. They may declare no `uses`. Naming an operation outside a hook's column is a load error. `event.params` takes `thinking`, `effort`, `temperature`, and `max_output_tokens`. dal clamps them to the model's limits. `preview` holds at most 4 KiB of the result.

A verdict is valid only for the event that made it. Returning `None`, a dictionary, or another event's verdict from a deciding hook is a failure, not an implicit allow. A failed `tool_call` hook blocks the call. A failed `input`, `before_turn`, or `before_request` hook changes nothing. dal records a failed observer and leaves the result unchanged.

Hooks run in one fixed order: built-ins, then bundled plugins by name, then your plugins by name. Inside one plugin, hooks run in list order. A `rewrite` feeds the next hook. The first `block` or `handled` ends the chain. One exception applies: on `input`, a built-in `handled` still lets later origins run. `before_turn` texts join with a blank line.

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def guard_patch(ctx, event):
    if event.tool == "patch" and ctx.config.read_only:
        return event.block("Patch is disabled by this plugin's policy.")
    return event.allow()

def remember(ctx, event):
    record = ctx.state.read(key = "last_tool")
    ctx.state.write(key = "last_tool", value = event.tool, expected = record.revision)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "policy",
    version = "0.1.0",
    config = dal.schema(read_only = dal.boolean(default = False)),
    hooks = [
        dal.on("tool_call", guard_patch),
        dal.on("tool_result", remember, uses = ["state.read", "state.write"]),
    ],
)
```

This hook blocks `patch` by name. It does not stop `exec` from writing a file. A hook is policy, not a boundary. The boundary is the approval ladder and the sandbox.

## Read settings

`config = dal.schema(...)` declares the settings. Values come from the `[plugin.<name>]` table in `dal.toml`:

```toml
[plugin.policy]
read_only = true
```

The handler reads `ctx.config.read_only`. An unknown key, a wrong type, or an invalid default fails at load, before any handler runs. Read an optional setting with `getattr(ctx.config, "name", dal.MISSING)`. A plugin gets settings only this way.

## Add skills, rules, and prompt text

`dal.skill(description, path)` publishes a skill. The path is relative to the plugin directory, so dal reads `skills/review/SKILL.md` when the plugin loads. `letter2image = True` turns on letter handling for the skill. The [system prompt](prompt.md) page describes letter handling. Skills collide by name. A clashing record is not published. An ambiguous short name refuses to resolve. A clash without an explicit replacement is refused.

A user plugin can take over one bundled skill or rule by naming it explicitly. The mechanism is shared in dal; in dalgona the bundled owners include `skills` and `quality`. Only `skill` and `rule` records are replaceable. The extension name itself is never replaceable.

`dal.skill(..., replace = True, battery = "<bundled extension>")` and `dal.rule(..., replace = True, battery = "<bundled extension>")` carry the claim as one inseparable pair. Omitting the pair, or writing `replace = False`, keeps the default refusal of a clashing record. `replace` is a boolean and `battery` is a string; an explicit `None` for either is a wrong-type refusal at the declaring call, not an omission. Writing `battery` without `replace = True`, or `replace = True` without `battery`, is a strict input refusal at the call that names both keywords.

The owner is never implied and must name the bundled extension exactly. A name no bundled extension ships, a bundled extension that does not register the record, a built-in extension, or a user plugin each refuses the load. Naming the wrong bundled extension refuses even when another bundled extension registers the record. A record another user plugin already replaced refuses as well. A plugin named like a battery stays rejected even with the pair.

A replacement moves one record and nothing else. The replacing extension keeps its own plain user identity and inherits no extension name, service request, tool, prompt section, status kind, or grant from the owner.

A skill that replaces the bundled `find-anything` skill owned by `skills`:

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "mine",
    version = "0.1.0",
    skills = {
        "find-anything": dal.skill(
            description = "Mine replaces the bundled finder.",
            path = "skills/find-anything/SKILL.md",
            replace = True,
            battery = "skills",
        ),
    },
)
```

A rule that replaces the bundled `fabricated-unavailable-tool-call` rule owned by `quality`:

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "mine",
    version = "0.1.0",
    rules = {
        "fabricated-unavailable-tool-call": dal.rule(
            pattern = "\\bfoo\\b",
            text = "Mine replaces the bundled detector.",
            replace = True,
            battery = "quality",
        ),
    },
)
```

Reload rebuilds the declared owners. Removing the claim and renaming or deleting the user record restores the bundled original. Keeping the colliding record without the claim refuses the reload and the previous plugin set stays live.

`dal.rule(text, pattern, judge, always_apply, scope, interrupt_mode, repeat_mode, repeat_gap)` publishes a rule. Every argument is a keyword. Only `text` is required. A rule with a `pattern` watches the model's output. The `pattern` is a regular expression. On a match, dal tells the model the `text`. A rule with `always_apply = True` and no `pattern` applies every turn. A rule needs a pattern unless it always applies. A rule with neither fails at the call. `judge` is optional instruction text for judged rules.

The last four arguments narrow where and how often a rule fires. Leave one out to keep the `[rules]` default.

| Argument | Values |
| --- | --- |
| `scope` | a list of `text`, `thinking`, `tool`, or `tool:<name>`, such as `["tool:exec"]` |
| `interrupt_mode` | `always`, `prose-only`, `tool-only`, or `never` |
| `repeat_mode` | `once` or `after-gap` |
| `repeat_gap` | a whole number from 1 to 1000 |

A value outside these lists stops the plugin from loading. The error names the argument and the values to use. Rules, the `[rules]` settings, and the judged-rule gate are on the [Rules](rules.md) page.

`prompt` is one fixed section of the system prompt.

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "style",
    version = "0.1.0",
    prompt = "Prefer small, reviewable changes.",
    skills = {
        "review": dal.skill(
            description = "Review a diff for missing tests. Use when the user asks for a review.",
            path = "skills/review/SKILL.md",
        ),
    },
    rules = {
        "no-todo": dal.rule(
            pattern = "\\bTODO\\b",
            text = "Finish the TODO now, or say why it stays.",
            scope = ["text", "tool:patch"],
            repeat_mode = "after-gap",
            repeat_gap = 10,
        ),
        "small-diffs": dal.rule(
            text = "Keep each change small enough to review at a glance.",
            always_apply = True,
        ),
    },
)
```

## Call a plugin tool from eval

An `eval` cell can call a published tool as `tools["<plugin>.<key>"]`. The cell needs both the tool's id and the operations that tool declares:

```starlark
tools["quality.todos"](path = "src")
```

That cell needs `tools.quality.todos` and `tools.search` in its operations. [Tools, modes, and approval](tools.md#the-eval-tool) explains how a cell gets them.

## Load, reload, and errors

Load has no compile step. A broken plugin stops startup and names `path:line:col`. Load is all or nothing. One bad plugin stops the whole set. Type `/reload` to re-evaluate the plugins. It prints counts, for example `Reloaded 2 plugins: 3 tools. New turns use them. A running turn keeps the plugins it started with.` On failure, it prints `reload failed: <rendered error>` on one line and `the previous plugin set stays live` on the next.

Plugins come from the data root only, never from the workspace. A plugin that loads in dalgon loads in dalgona. See `dalgona://batteries` for the batteries product.

## Declare scripted models

A plugin can declare `models` with `dal.model(id = ..., caps = ..., run = ..., uses = [...])`. A scripted model that runs where no script context exists fails with `script context is unavailable for this model`. To call a model from a tool, request `models.infer`.

    ("prompt", "# The system prompt

The system prompt is the text dal sends to the model before your first message. Dal builds it from parts. Plugins, skills, and rules add to it.

Use this page to see what the model reads and which parts you can extend.

## The parts

The prompt assembles in this order: identity, D2, tools, skills, rules, rulebook, plugins, environment, instructions, fallback, docs line.

| part | what it holds |
|---|---|
| identity | one paragraph: `You are dal <version>, a coding agent. Work in the current directory. Read files before you edit them. Keep responses short and factual. Finish the whole task before you report.` |
| D2 | the line `D2 is preferred for diagrams.` |
| tools | a `<tools>` block with one line for each tool: `- <name>: <description>` |
| skills | the skill list |
| rules and rulebook | the rules that always apply, then the rulebook text |
| plugins | the `prompt` text of each plugin that sets one |
| docs line | `Read dal://index with the read tool when the user asks about dal itself.` |

The tools block is left out when no tool is listed. This page lists the parts. Read it from the terminal with `dalgon docs dal://prompt`.

## Add text from a plugin

A plugin adds one fixed section to the plugins part. Set `prompt` in `plugin.star`. The model reads the text as written.

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "style",
    version = "0.1.0",
    prompt = "Prefer small, reviewable changes.",
)
```

[Plugins](plugins.md#add-skills-rules-and-prompt-text) shows `prompt`, `skills`, and `rules` in one plugin.

## Skills and letters

Skill descriptions appear in the prompt or as a letter. Letters carry long stable text as images. You can read the exact text at `letter://<id>`. A description that cannot be drawn falls back to text.

## AGENTS.md and SYSTEM.md

The prompt has a slot for user instructions. The prompt code can render that slot from `AGENTS.md` files and a `SYSTEM.md` file. It labels each `AGENTS.md` as `# Instructions from <path>`, root first. It adds the `SYSTEM.md` text from the data root with no label. Instructions are context for the model. They never act as a permission boundary.

The session driver does not pass `AGENTS.md` or `SYSTEM.md` text to this slot yet. A file you create for them does not reach the model.

## Font license

This product bundles GNU Unifont 18.0.01 glyph data for letter images. Upstream offers the font under the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1, and GNU GPL version 2 or later with the GNU Font Embedding Exception. This distribution uses the SIL Open Font License, Version 1.1. Read the full bundled terms at dal://license under the appendix “Third-party font: GNU Unifont 18.0.01”. Upstream: https://unifoundry.com/unifont/.

## Next

- [Rules](rules.md) explains always rules, rulebook files, and stream rules.
- [Plugins](plugins.md#add-skills-rules-and-prompt-text) shows how a plugin adds skills, rules, and prompt text.

    ("protocol", "# dal JSON-RPC protocol reference

The dal protocol lets another process drive dal. Use it to build a GUI, an editor integration, or a test harness on the same operations that the terminal uses. Run `dalgon rpc` to serve it. This page lists the methods, the rules for each method group, and the rules for updates.

Each frame is one JSON-RPC 2.0 message on one line, ended by a line feed. A frame holds at most 16777216 bytes. A larger frame ends the connection. Frames run over stdio or a local socket. `initialize` negotiates capabilities. The protocol version is 1. A client that can answer approval requests lists `approval` in its `initialize` capabilities. A client that can answer extension questions lists `question`. A session with no such client attached denies approvals. It gives questions their default answer at once.

| method | params | result | capability |
|---|---|---|---|
| initialize | protocolVersion, capabilities | ready | none |
| protocol/schema | none | schema | none |
| commands/list | none | commands | none |
| session/list | limit, cursor, search | sessions | sessions |
| session/open | ref | session | sessions |
| session/close | sessionId | ok | sessions |
| session/view | sessionId, limit, before | view | sessions |
| session/subscribe | sessionId, gen, after | stream | sessions |
| session/unsubscribe | sessionId | ok | sessions |
| session/submit | sessionId, command | reply | sessions |
| session/answer | sessionId, requestId, answer | ok | sessions |
| blob/read | sessionId, blobId | bytes | blobs |
| models/list | none | models | models |
| docs/read | uri | text | docs |
| host/subscribe | none | stream | host.updates |
| host/unsubscribe | none | ok | host.updates |
| auth/status | none | providers | auth |
| auth/login | provider, method, apiKey | pending, then ok | auth |
| auth/cancel | loginId | cancelled | auth |
| auth/logout | provider | removed | auth |

## Start a connection

Run `dalgon rpc`. Send `initialize` as the first request. A request before `initialize` fails with `-32006` and the message `initialize must be the first request`. A second `initialize` fails with `-32600`. Only `protocol/schema` may come first.

Write this line to standard input:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":1,"capabilities":["sessions"],"clientInfo":{"name":"demo"}}}
```

The server writes one line back. It names the protocol version, the server, the capabilities it accepted, and your client id. In this reply, `<version>` is the server version and `<n>` is a connection number:

```text
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"protocolVersion":1,"serverInfo":{"name":"dal","version":"<version>"},"capabilities":["sessions"],"clientId":"demo#<n>"}}
```

The reply lists only the capabilities that the server supports and that you asked for. It never echoes `approval` or `question`. A method that needs a capability you did not get fails with `-32007` and the message `capability "<name>" is not enabled on this connection`.

## Request rules

Requests need exactly one answer. Blobs are content-addressed. Error codes follow JSON-RPC. `experimental/` methods may change.

## Authentication methods

An `auth/login` with `method` `browser` or `device` answers `pending` with the `loginId` and `url` (and `userCode` for `device`) as soon as the provider flow reports one. When the flow ends, the host publishes one `login_finished` host update naming the attempt's `loginId`. `method` `api_key` takes the key in `apiKey`. It answers `ok` after the key is stored. `auth/cancel` takes the `loginId` of a pending login. It cancels the attempt. It answers whether one was still pending. `auth/status` lists each provider as `ready`, `not_configured`, or `expired`. `auth/logout` without `provider` removes every stored credential. A `provider` that is present but not a string is refused with `-32602`. The host removes nothing.

## Error handling

Seven methods decode their params strictly: `auth/login`, `auth/cancel`, `auth/logout`, `session/list`, `session/view`, `session/subscribe`, and `docs/read`. In them, an omitted optional member selects its default. A present member of the wrong type (or non-object params) is refused with `-32602`. Members that take no default stay required (`provider` and `method` for `auth/login`, `sessionId` wherever used). Invalid parameter errors format their message as `invalid params for <method>: <detail>` with code `-32602`. ACP `session/list` accepts null `cwd` and `cursor` filters.

## Session commands

`session/submit` takes every command type the `Command` decoder knows. An unknown `type` is refused with `-32602`. `session/submit` refuses an `export` command whose path is absolute or climbs with `..`. It answers `-32602` and writes no file. Relative paths inside the workspace and the default target stay valid.

### Chooser replies

A command may reply with `choose` (`{"type":"choose","chooser":<name>,"filter":<string>}`) asking the client to display an interactive picker. For `chooser` `"thinking"`, the reply carries an optional `thinkingLevels` array listing the canonical level names supported by the active model:

```json
{"type":"choose","chooser":"thinking","filter":"","thinkingLevels":["off","minimal","low","medium","high","xhigh","max"]}
```

`thinkingLevels` is included only when `chooser` is `"thinking"`. For all other choosers (`model`, `settings`, `scoped_models`, `session`, `tree`, `fork_point`, `login`, `logout`), `thinkingLevels` is omitted.

When `thinkingLevels` is omitted from the wire, the deserializer preserves the field as absent, treating capability information as unsupported rather than guessing supported levels. When `thinkingLevels` is present as an explicit empty array (`[]`), the active model supports no thinking levels. When the user selects a level, the client submits that selection as a `/thinking <level>` command rather than setting the level directly, allowing the host to validate the choice against its model capabilities.

## Updates

Updates carry `seq` and `gen`. Clients resync on gaps.

## Extension status

An extension that registers a status kind reports changes as `ext_status` updates with `ext`, `state` (`busy` or `quiet`), and optional `text`. For example: `{"type":"ext_status","ext":"focus","state":"busy","text":"indexing"}` and `{"type":"ext_status","ext":"focus","state":"quiet"}`. The host polls each kind on a short fixed interval. It sends an update only when the state or text changes. A quiet extension with no text is the starting state. It sends nothing until it has been busy. A fresh wire subscription has no status seed. It receives changes as they occur. An embedded client reads the current busy or text-bearing statuses with `Agent::ext_status`. ACP clients receive the same change as a `_dal/notice` with `kind` `status` and the text `<ext>: <text>`, `<ext>: busy`, or `<ext>: quiet`. A2A streams carry it as the `dal.status` metadata of a status update. The router sends nothing. `dalgon --json` writes its result line only after every status kind is quiet.

## Shutdown

A server that is stopping answers each new request with `-32009` (`server_draining`). It gives running requests one second to finish. Then it closes the connection.

## Model rows

Each `models/list` row carries `id`, `provider`, `name`, and an optional `contextWindow`. `provider` is the label of the row's API family. Every chat and responses provider reads `openai`. It does not name a configured provider. Two rows can therefore share `id` and `provider`. Each row also carries `route`, the typed route that selects exactly that row, and an optional `reference`:

| Row | `route` | `reference` |
|---|---|---|
| API model with a known provider | `{"kind":"api","family":..,"model":..,"provider":..}` | `provider/model` |
| API model without a known provider | the same without `provider` | absent |
| Synthetic or harness model | `{"kind":"synthetic","id":..}` or `{"kind":"harness","id":..}` | the id |

A client that selects a row submits its `route` in `set_model`. It submits nothing it rebuilt from `id` or `provider`. A server that predates `route` and `reference` omits them. A client then keeps its older selection by name. That name cannot tell same-family providers apart. A member that is present but malformed is an error, not an absent member. `auth/status` rows and the protocol version 1 are unchanged.

## Assistant entries

Assistant entries carry one `model` identifier. Their optional `route` member identifies the route that produced the response:

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `{"api":"openai_chat"}` | An API route, with its API family. The other family values are `openai_responses`, `openai_codex`, and `anthropic`. |
| `"synthetic"` | A named synthetic model. |
| `"harness"` | A built-in harness mode. |

The route describes the existing `model` identifier. Its API family is independent of the entry's top-level `api` member, which describes the provider wire format. New responses include `route`. An absent member means the route is unknown, not that it is an API route. The decoder rejects `null`, unknown route kinds, and model identifiers that do not fit the declared synthetic or harness kind.

`protocol/schema` includes this optional, non-null member. Protocol version 1 and the format-1 encoding of assistant entries remain unchanged. Turn-ID reservations use journal format 2 and mail deliveries use journal format 3. See [durable turn identities](sessions.md#durable-turn-identities).

## Next

- [Build a client on the dal protocol](integrate.md): connect a program through `dalgon rpc`.
- [Embed dal in a Rust program](sdk.md): call the same operations in process.
- [Command line](cli.md): start `dalgon rpc`, `dalgon acp`, or `dalgon serve`.

    ("quickstart", "# Quickstart: run your first dal agent turn

Dal is a coding agent for your terminal. This page takes you from a source build to one answered prompt and one approved edit.

You sign in once. Dal stores the credentials and reuses them in every workspace. Dal asks before it edits a file or runs a command, so you can try it on a real repository.

## Before you start

You need:

- git.
- The latest stable Rust toolchain from rustup.
- A C toolchain. The symbol grammars compile through `cc`.
- An account or an API key for one provider.

## Install

Build from source. No tagged release exists, so the registry and installer channels have nothing to fetch yet. [Install](install.md) lists the platform details.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/gosuda/dalgona
cd dalgona
rustup update stable --no-self-update
cargo build --release --locked -p dalgon -p dalgona
export PATH="$PWD/target/release:$PATH"
```

In PowerShell, use `$env:PATH = "$PWD\target\release;$env:PATH"` for the last line.

Check the install. `dalgon --version` prints `dalgon` and the package version. `dal` and `dl` are aliases of `dalgon`.

```sh
dalgon --version
```

## Sign in

Run the sign-in command in a terminal.

```sh
dalgon login
```

Dal lists the providers it can sign in to. Type the number or the id of one provider. Press Enter. An empty line cancels.

- A provider with browser or device sign-in prints a URL. A device sign-in also prints a code. Follow the lines dal prints. Dal waits until the sign-in ends.
- A provider with an API key asks for the key. Dal masks what you type. It then prints `Saved <name> credentials. Run dal to pick a model.`

To sign in without a prompt, pipe the key and name the provider:

```sh
printf %s "$KEY" | dalgon login anthropic --api-key
```

A provider also counts as signed in when its key variable is set, such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `OPENAI_API_KEY`.

Check the result:

```sh
dalgon login status
```

Each line names a provider and its state: `ready`, `expired`, or `not configured`. The command exits 0 when at least one provider is ready. Otherwise it exits 1 and prints `Run dalgon login <provider> to sign in.` on stderr.

Dalgona keeps its own data root, including its sign-in. Run `dalgona login` to sign it in.

## Pick a model

Dal needs a model before it can answer. Start dal in your project directory.

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
dalgon
```

Dal shows `No model selected yet. dal needs a model before it can answer.` Type `/model` and press Enter. Dal lists the models of the providers you signed in to. Type to filter the list. Move with the arrow keys. Press Enter to pick a model. Press Esc to cancel. Dal saves your pick as the default model in `dal.toml`.

To pick a model without the terminal interface, list the models. Then pass one as `PROVIDER/ID`, joining the first two columns of a row with a slash.

```sh
dalgon models
dalgon -m PROVIDER/ID -p "Summarize this repository's README"
```

You can also set `model = "PROVIDER/ID"` in `dal.toml`. See [Install](install.md#config-and-data-roots) for the file path and [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) for the keys.

## Run your first turn

Print mode runs one turn without the terminal interface. It writes the answer to stdout and exits.

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
dalgon -p "Summarize this repository's README"
```

Without a model, print mode stops with `dalgon: no model is configured: dal.toml has no model key and --model was not given`. Pick a model first.

For a conversation, run `dalgon` and type a prompt. Press Enter to send. Press Esc to interrupt a running turn. Press F1 for key help. Type `/quit` to leave. [Terminal and keys](terminal.md) lists every key.

Dal saves the session. Continue it later with `dalgon -c`.

## Approve a change

The default approval mode is `ask`. Dal asks before every `patch` and every `exec`.

In the terminal, ask for a small edit:

```text
Create notes.txt that contains one line of text.
```

Before dal edits the file, it shows a prompt titled `Allow this edit to <path>?`. Press `y` to allow the edit once. Press `a` to allow for this session. Press `n` or Esc to deny. The answer keys unlock a moment after the prompt opens. The prompt also offers View full preview. A shell command gets the title `Allow this command?`.

Print mode cannot ask. Under `ask`, it denies `patch` and `exec` calls. When the model calls `patch`, print mode prints these lines on stderr:

```text
dalgon: approval is ask and no terminal is attached: patch and exec calls are denied. Re-run with --approval all to approve them.
dalgon: patch needs approval; print mode cannot ask. Rerun with --approval edits.
dalgon: 1 call denied by approval mode.
```

Pass `--approval edits` to allow edits in print mode. `exec` still needs `--approval all`. Use `all` only inside an external sandbox. The built-in `--sandbox` sets no network restriction. See [Sandbox](sandbox.md).

## What you did

You built dal, signed in, picked a model, ran one turn, and answered one approval prompt.

## Next

- [Tools, modes, and approval](tools.md) explains the approval ladder and the `eval` tool.
- [Sessions and compaction](sessions.md) covers `-c`, `-r`, and `-n`.
- [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) lists every key.
- [Command line](cli.md) lists the subcommands and exit codes.
- [Plugins](plugins.md) shows how to write your first plugin.

    ("requirements", "# Product requirements (maintainer spec)

This page is the maintainer spec, not a user guide. To use dal, start with [Quickstart](quickstart.md). To learn why dal has this shape, read [Philosophy](philosophy.md).

Every requirement in this document is a mandatory obligation that dal and dalgona must satisfy. Unmet obligations stand as requirements to implement and verify rather than claims of completed proof.

## Platform and architecture

dal must be a complete and fully usable coding agent platform on its own.
dal must maintain a minimal expandable core with no private interior.
Every capability beyond the core loop must register through the public extension door.
The primary binary must be dalgon.
dal and dl must be identical aliases.
dalgona must extend dal through the public extension door.
It must supply opinionated batteries.
The repository and all workspace packages must inherit the Sustainable Use License Version 1.0 with licensor metaphorics.
Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows on x86_64 and aarch64 must attach to release assets.

## Seams and protocols

In process, the host-agent seam must provide five operations over one snapshot: read, change stream, command path, request-response, and blob read.
Across processes, dal must serve a JSON-RPC protocol over standard input/output and local sockets that matches the in-process seam.
dal serve must bind to loopback by default without authentication.
Public endpoints must bind all interfaces and require a token.
Headless JSON mode must emit one prompt result on success or one JSON-RPC error object on failure, without streaming handshakes.
dal must support inline terminal, fullscreen terminal user interface, headless print, headless JSON, ACP, RPC, router, and A2A interfaces.
The ACP server must support protocolVersion 1 and protocolVersion 2.
The A2A interface must support version 1.0 over JSON-RPC and HTTP+JSON when started with the --a2a flag.

## Extension and plugin system

dal must evaluate plugins from Starlark scripts at load time with no compilation step.
dal must load user plugins only from the user data directory under plugins.
Workspace directories must never load plugins.
Plugins must declare required capabilities in a deny-by-default manifest.
The host must grant only user-approved capabilities.
Plugins must be able to register tools, slash commands, skills, rules, and prompt sections through the extension door.
First-party extensions must register documentation pages through the shared extension builder.
Plugins must hook into lifecycle events with declared result types: tool calls, user input, turn boundaries, and session lifecycle.
A plugin load failure must halt startup.
It must report the file, line, and column.
Slash command /reload must evaluate fresh plugins without damage to live state if evaluation fails.
One extension software development kit must serve dal and dalgona.
A plugin that loads in dalgon must load in dalgona.
dal must document a conversion workflow to port external TypeScript extensions to Starlark plugins.

## Session journal and state

dal must store sessions as append-only journals that sync to disk on each change.
A record must count as saved only after fsync.
Session histories must form trees.
Resuming with -r or continuing with -c must preserve tree leaves and branches.
Slash commands /tree, /fork, and /clone must inspect and branch session histories.
Slash command /export must write a standalone session transcript file.
Context compaction must run automatically at 85 percent of the context window by default.
It must run remote compaction before local summarization.
Long or stable text may project as image letters.
The exact source text must remain retrievable at letter://<id>.

## Tools and approval

Every mode must provide the read, search, patch, exec, and eval tools.
Eval-first and eval-only modes must also reach plugin tools and prompt sections marked eval_only.
The eval tool must run Starlark only.
An operation denied outside eval must be denied inside eval.
eval must not be treated as a sandbox.
The patch tool must support multiple edit styles.
The default is anchor in dal and hashline in dalgona.
The patch edit style must follow the active model per request when configured in the per-model table.
The approval ladder must follow --approval ask|edits|all.
By default, dal asks before each patch and each exec.
When no person can answer an approval prompt, dal must deny the operation and record the reason.
Read-only tool calls must batch in parallel.
Mutating patch and exec calls must run one at a time in request order.
Long foreground commands must detach into background jobs to preserve interactive control.
Tool execution may carry scoped command prefix grants valid for the active job.
An optional sandbox must guard home files outside allowed paths, with no network restriction.

## Code intelligence and syntax operations

Symbol search must use Tree-sitter to extract definitions from on-disk parses across supported programming languages.
Search mode symbol must list matching definitions, outline single files, and reveal single matches with def tags.
The patch tool must support definition replacement and relative insertion by symbol name and def tag.
Hashline block edits must use the N* operator to address outermost syntactic blocks when symbol search is enabled.
dal must not include a language server protocol client.
Code intelligence must consist of bounded search, syntax walks, and structural patch.

## Prompt construction and provider integration

The system prompt must assemble from AGENTS.md files, SYSTEM.md, active skills, rules, and plugin sections.
TTSR stream rules must inspect model output streams, match patterns, interrupt generation, inject rules, and retry.
dal must connect to four provider families: OpenAI Chat, OpenAI Responses, OpenAI Codex, and Anthropic.
Session commands /model and /thinking must change the model and reasoning effort during a session.
Thinking levels must include off, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max.
Luna Reserve must operate on the Codex provider as an opt-in model.
It must never be a default model.
Provider and protocol replies must decode tolerantly to support upstream schema evolution.

## Terminal user interface

Text measurement must match terminal drawing cell widths.
It must never split multi-byte or wide characters.
The terminal user interface must support inline scrollback and alternate-screen fullscreen modes.
The terminal user interface must render native diagrams for D2, Nomnoml, DOT, and Mermaid formats.
Terminal themes must provide sufficient contrast to satisfy accessibility contrast standards.

## Self-documentation system

One resolver must serve documentation over immutable pages under dal:// and dalgona:// schemes.
Documentation URIs must follow the grammar scheme://page with lowercase segments and no traversal syntax.
Every page must be valid UTF-8 Markdown with a title on line one.
It must stay under 49152 bytes and 1500 lines.
Slash command /docs and read tool scheme reads must render manual pages without line numbers or edit footers.
Failed page lookups must provide nearest suggestions within an edit distance of two.

## Guard and batteries

The core must ship a lean judge component with configurable model roles, typed judgment, and auto|on|off gating.
In dal the judge must feed judged rules and eval batching.
dalgona must enable all judge-fed capabilities by default.
dalgona must ship batteries for web search and fetch, plan and todo, a rich questionnaire tool, an MCP client, and a review loop.
dalgona must enable the anti-complexity and anti-slop guard by default.
dal must keep the guard disabled by default.
The guard must measure growth deltas, absolute metrics, metric deltas, and current bests.
It must block only deterministic invalid content.

## Concurrency and resource bounds

dal must maintain structured concurrency with explicit ownership, race-free state transitions, and no leaked threads or processes.
Concurrency invariants and lock ordering must be verifiable under deterministic permutation tests.
Configuration parsing must deny unknown fields and report the exact offending line in dal.toml.
Under high load, the system must bound memory growth, manage open file descriptors, and maintain responsive keypress echo latency.

## Next

- [Philosophy](philosophy.md): read why dal has one extension door.
- [Tools, modes, and approval](tools.md): read how the tool and approval rules behave today.

    ("rules", "# Rules: stream, always, and rulebook

Three kinds of rules exist. Stream rules watch output. Always rules apply every turn. Rulebook files hold project rules. User rule files live under `<data-root>/rules/`. Project rule files live under `<workspace>/.dal/rules/`. Enabled plugins can also supply files from their `rules/` directories. Read a rule at `rule://<name>`.

## Interrupts and retries

Stream rules can interrupt a response and supply a reminder for the retry. `rules.max_retries` caps these interrupts per turn. At the cap, unjudged matches supply reminders without interrupting. Judged matches become report-only: they do not call the judge or add a reminder. A report-only rule never interrupts.

dal writes rule reminders to the session journal before delivery. They enter model context and its token estimate. They remain available when you resume the session. A session keeps its captured rule set. Editing a rule file does not change an already-open session.

## Judged rules

A judged rule has a pattern and a yes-or-no judge question. Session startup checks the selected judge route and its credentials without generating a response or consuming a scripted response. Readiness does not guarantee that a later model request will succeed.

`rules.judge` controls which judged rules enter the session's matching set:

- `off` excludes judged rules.
- `auto` includes them when the shared judge is ready. Otherwise, it excludes them and reports a readiness note.
- `on` requires a ready shared judge. If none is ready, session startup fails.

The shared judge has a separate `gate` setting under `[judge]`. Setting `judge.gate = "off"` skips its readiness check. Setting `rules.judge = "off"` does not disable the shared judge, which other features can use. If either gate is `on`, an unavailable judge prevents startup. dal returns unexpected readiness errors. It does not treat them as missing credentials.

When a judged match can interrupt, dal closes the provider stream before requesting the verdict:

- `true` confirms a violation. dal records the rule fire and retries with its reminder.
- `false` rejects the match. dal reports one informational pass note and retries without a rule fire or reminder.
- A judge error or timeout reports one informational failure note and retries without a rule fire or reminder.

dal latches the rule for that turn before the verdict wait. A retry does not judge the same rule again. Cancellation stops the wait without a late rule fire or retry. The configured retry cap still applies.

See [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) for rule defaults.

## Next

- [Settings in dal.toml](config.md): set `rules.judge` and the other rule defaults.
