    ("config", "# Settings in dal.toml

The file is `dal.toml` under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dal/` (default `~/.config/dal/dal.toml`). Data lives under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dal/`. Layering: code defaults, then product defaults, then user `dal.toml`, then CLI flags. A later layer replaces an earlier value by key path. `dalgona` reads `dal.toml` under `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dalgona/` with data under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dalgona/`.

The table shows dal's built-in defaults before product TOML, user settings, and CLI overrides. The meaning column identifies dalgona's different defaults. `none` means omit the key, not the TOML string `"none"`. An omitted table still uses the field defaults listed below. Replace `<data-root>` with your product's data directory.

| key | type | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `mode` | string | `normal` | harness mode: `normal`, `eval-first`, or `eval-only`; `--mode` overrides it for one run; see [Tools](tools.md) |
| `model` | string | `none` | the default model reference; dal writes it when you pick a model; `-m` overrides it for one run |
| `thinking` | string | `medium` | the default reasoning level: `off`, `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, or `max`; `--thinking` overrides it for one run |
| `approval` | string | `ask` | the approval policy for `patch` and `exec`: `ask` asks before each call, `edits` approves edits and asks for `exec`, `all` approves every call; `--approval` overrides it for one run; see [Tools](tools.md) |
| `screen` | string | `inline` | the terminal surface: `inline` keeps terminal scrollback; `fullscreen` uses the alternate screen and replays the settled transcript on exit; `--screen` overrides it for one run; see [Terminal](terminal.md) |
| `theme` | string | `auto` | the terminal colors: `auto` follows the terminal background, `palette` uses the terminal's own palette, or name one of the nine shipped themes, such as `catppuccin-mocha` |
| `sandbox` | bool | `false` | `true` runs every `exec` child through the platform sandbox; `--sandbox` turns it on for one run; see [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `images` | bool | `false` | `true` enables inline images in terminals that support an image protocol; diagrams render as text when images are off |
| `motion` | bool | `true` | `false` turns off repeated terminal motion; the `DAL_NO_MOTION` environment variable turns it off too |
| `compact_ratio` | number | `0.85` | the share of the context window at which compaction starts, from `0.5` to `0.95`; `0.85` means 85 percent; see [Sessions](sessions.md) |
| `edit_style` | string | `anchor` | the patch format; dalgona defaults to `hashline` |
| `guard` | table | `{ enabled = false }` | guard settings; dalgona defaults to `enabled = true`; see [Guard](guard.md) |
| `search_symbols` | bool | `false` | whether search includes symbols; dalgona defaults to `true` |
| `judge` | table | `none` | shared judge settings, including `gate`; readiness checks do not generate a response; see [Judged rules](rules.md#judged-rules) |
| `plugins` | list | `[]` | the names of the plugins to load; each name is a directory under `<data-root>/plugins/` that holds a `plugin.star`; see [Plugins](plugins.md) |
| `aliases` | table | `none` | short names for models; each key is an alias and each value is a non-empty model id; `-m` accepts an alias |
| `serve` | table | `none` | local control endpoint settings; field defaults apply when omitted |
| `serve.bind` | string | `127.0.0.1` | the address the router binds; `--bind` overrides it; an address that is not loopback needs `--public` and a token |
| `serve.port` | number | `7437` | the TCP port the router listens on, from 0 to 65535; `--port` overrides it |
| `serve.token_file` | path | `"<data-root>/serve.token"` | the authentication token file |
| `serve.approval` | string | `ask` | the approval policy for requests that reach the endpoint: `ask`, `edits`, or `all`; it follows `approval` when you leave it unset |
| `serve.origins` | list | `[]` | the browser origins that may open a WebSocket to the endpoint; write each origin exactly; a WebSocket upgrade that carries any other `Origin` header gets `403` |
| `prices` | table | `none` | per-model prices in USD per million tokens, one `prices.<model-id>` table per model; a price set here wins over the compiled price table; each table needs all four rates, and each rate is a number that is not negative |
| `prices.<model-id>.input` | number | `none` | the rate for uncached input tokens; required in each `prices.<model-id>` table |
| `prices.<model-id>.cached_input` | number | `none` | the rate for cached input tokens; required |
| `prices.<model-id>.cache_write` | number | `none` | the `prices.<model-id>.cache_write` setting; `none` keeps the historical fallback to the applicable input rate |
| `prices.<model-id>.output` | number | `none` | the rate for output tokens, not counting reasoning tokens; required |
| `prices.<model-id>.reasoning` | number | `none` | the rate for separately reported reasoning tokens; required; a rate of `0` is a known price |
| `prices.<model-id>.tiers` | list | `[]` | request-wide context tiers in any order; each tier has `size` (input threshold) and optional `input`, `cached_input`, `cache_write`, `output`, `reasoning` overrides |
| `rules` | table | `none` | rule matching and retry settings; field defaults apply when omitted |
| `rules.watch` | bool | `true` | whether to watch stream rules |
| `rules.interrupt` | string | `always` | interrupt mode when a rule does not set its own |
| `rules.repeat` | string | `once` | repeat mode when a rule does not set its own |
| `rules.repeat_gap` | number | `10` | turn gap for `after-gap` repeats |
| `rules.max_retries` | number | `3` | maximum rule interrupts per turn |
| `rules.disabled` | list | `[]` | the rule names to drop before rule sets are built, such as `no-sleep`; a name starts with a letter or digit and has at most 64 characters from letters, digits, `.`, `_`, and `-` |
| `rules.judge` | string | `auto` | `off` excludes judged rules; `auto` includes them only when the judge is ready; `on` requires readiness at session startup; separate from `judge.gate`; see [Judged rules](rules.md#judged-rules) |
| `sandbox_writable` | list | `[]` | extra directories that stay writable under the sandbox; each entry is an absolute path or starts with `~/`, and it must exist; it cannot hold the home directory or overlap the dal config and data roots; see [Sandbox](sandbox.md) |
| `agents` | table | `none` | child-session settings: `enabled` publishes the `agent` model tool, `max_concurrent` caps running children, `max_depth` caps nesting; see below |
| `limits` | table | `none` | the Starlark budgets under `limits.plugins`; see below |
| `models` | table | `none` | provider-layer defaults: `default`, `thinking`, and `aliases`; see below |
| `retry` | table | `none` | provider retry limits: `request_max_retries` and `stream_max_retries`; see below |
| `providers` | table | `none` | one `providers.<id>` table per provider; a built-in id changes that provider and any other id adds a named provider; see below |
| `ask` | table | `none` | holds one key, `timeout`; see `ask.timeout` |
| `ask.timeout` | string | `"30m"` | how long one raised question stays open; extension grant prompts ignore it and wait 120 s; clamped into `1m` to `120m` at load, with one startup notice naming the key, the value, and the clamp |
| `compact` | table | `none` | an extension-owned table that dal accepts without checking its keys; no part of dal reads a key from it; use `compact_ratio` to set when compaction starts |
| `rule_sets` | table | `none` | read by dalgona only: `rule_sets.enabled` lists the bundled rule sets to load; dal accepts the table and reads no key from it; see `dalgona://rules` |
| `plugin` | table | `none` | per-plugin settings, one `plugin.<name>` table per plugin; the plugin's `config` schema checks the table when the plugin loads; see [Plugins](plugins.md#read-settings) |
| `eval` | table | `none` | holds one key, `uses`; see `eval.uses` |
| `eval.uses` | list | `[]` | the operations that eval cells may request, such as `tools.read`, `tools.search`, `tools.patch`, `tools.exec`, `judge.ask`, `judge.batch`, or an exported `tools.<plugin>.<tool>`; each effect still goes through normal approval, with at most 64 entries and no wildcards or duplicates; empty means eval cells can only compute and cannot act |

`[aliases]` maps model aliases. `[serve]` holds router settings. `[limits]` holds run budgets. `[plugin.<name>]` holds per-plugin settings. `[providers.<id>]` configures named provider endpoints or overrides built-in provider routes.

A `[providers.<id>]` table sets connection and authentication settings:

- `api`: wire API family (`openai_chat`, `openai_responses`, `openai_codex`, `anthropic`, `bedrock`, `cursor`, `devin`, `droid`, `gitlab`, `google-generative-ai`, `google-vertex`, `google-gemini-cli`, `google-antigravity`, `mistral`, `ollama`, or `pi-messages`).
- `base_url`: endpoint base URL.
- `transport`: transport protocol, either `"https"` (default) or `"websocket"` (supported for `openai_responses` and `openai_codex`).
- `key_env`: name of the environment variable that holds the API key. Required for custom named providers unless `auth = "none"`. For built-in providers, `key_env` is optional and overrides the default environment variable.
- `auth`: authorization header style for API keys:
  - `"bearer"`: sends the key in an `Authorization: Bearer <key>` header (default for chat and responses).
  - `"x-api-key"`: sends the key in an `x-api-key: <key>` header (default for Anthropic).
  - `"api-key"`: sends the key in an `api-key: <key>` header.
  - `"none"`: sends no API-key authorization header; the entry carries no API key and builds no credential header. It does not make an OAuth-only family usable without its required credential: such a credential-less row is still refused at request admission.
- `max_concurrent_requests`: maximum simultaneous requests for this provider, between 1 and 64 (default 4).
- `api_version`: the `api-version` query value for an Azure-shaped entry. An entry value wins over `AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION`.
- `deployments`: a table mapping catalog model ids to Azure deployment names. An entry value wins model by model over `AZURE_OPENAI_DEPLOYMENT_NAME_MAP`; a model with no mapping is sent under its own id. Quote a model id that holds a dot (`"gpt-5.5" = "..."`), or TOML reads the dot as a table path.

## Tables with their own keys

These tables take more keys than the table above lists. An unknown key in any of them is an error.

- `[agents]`: `enabled` (default `false`) publishes the `agent` model tool. `max_concurrent` (default `32`) caps running children. `max_depth` (default `1`) caps nesting. Both caps are whole numbers above zero.
- `[limits.plugins]`: the Starlark budgets `load_ticks` (default `1000000`), `load_heap_bytes` (`16777216`), `handler_ticks` (`200000`), `handler_heap_bytes` (`8388608`), `cell_ticks` (`2000000`), `cell_heap_bytes` (`33554432`), and `stack_depth` (`100`). Each key holds one positive integer. The six tick and heap budgets accept `1` through `9223372036854775807`; `stack_depth` accepts `1` through `4294967295`. Zero, a negative, a fraction, a string, a boolean, or a list is refused as an invalid value that names the key and the accepted range. A missing key keeps its default. Each key named replaces only its default; layers merge per key.
- `[limits.plugins]` placement: the seven budget names directly under `[limits]` are refused and point at `limits.plugins.<name>`, for example `limits.load_ticks` suggests `limits.plugins.load_ticks`. The singular `[limits.plugin]` table is refused and points at `limits.plugins`. An unknown key inside `[limits.plugins]` is refused as an unknown key that names the full `limits.plugins.<name>` path, suggests the closest accepted spelling, and lists the seven accepted keys. A valid `[limits]` sibling such as `agents = 64`, and a valid `[agents]` table beside the budgets, stays legal.
- `[limits.plugins]` failures are actionable. A real load, handler, or eval-cell budget breach names the configured key with `raise limits.plugins.<key> to allow more`, alongside the applied budget and the vendor prefix (`Execution duration limit` for ticks, `Heap memory limit` for heap, `Starlark call stack overflow` for depth). `load_ticks` and `load_heap_bytes` guard plugin loading, `handler_ticks` and `handler_heap_bytes` guard one handler call, `cell_ticks` and `cell_heap_bytes` guard one eval cell, and the single `stack_depth` fans out to all three contexts. A user `fail()` that carries the vendor wording, or a source comment that mentions it, gains no remedy: the remedy appears only on a typed budget breach, never on a user failure or a source-text match.
- `[models]`: `default` is the model that an empty reference selects. `thinking` is a reasoning level (default `medium`). `aliases` maps short names to model references.
- `[retry]`: `request_max_retries` (default `4`) and `stream_max_retries` (default `5`). Each is a whole number from 0 to 100.
- `[providers.<id>]`: `api`, `base_url`, `transport` (`https` or `websocket`), `key_env`, `auth` (`bearer`, `x-api-key`, `api-key`, or `none`), and `max_concurrent_requests` (1 to 64, default `4`). Some providers also take `api_version`, `deployments`, `region`, `project`, `location`, `namespace`, `binary`, or `integration`. A new id needs `api` and `base_url`, and it needs `key_env` unless `auth` is `none`. The id `dal` is reserved.
- `[prices.<model-id>]`: besides the four rates, `cache_write` sets the cache-write rate. Without it, dal prices cache writes at the input rate. `tiers` is a non-empty array of tables for prompts above a context size. Each tier needs `size`, a context token count, and at least one rate: `input`, `cached_input`, `cache_write`, `output`, or `reasoning`. Tier sizes must strictly increase.
- `[ask]`: `timeout` only.

## Azure OpenAI

Azure is a shape on a Chat or Responses entry, not a separate `api` value: an entry with `auth = "api-key"`, an `api_version`, or a `deployments` table is sent through the Azure adapter. The key travels in an `api-key` header, never as `Bearer`; OAuth sign-in is refused for these entries.

For Azure entries, an explicit `base_url` always wins. When you omit it, `AZURE_OPENAI_BASE_URL` takes precedence over `AZURE_OPENAI_RESOURCE_NAME`. The resource name must be one valid DNS label, but dal does not validate it when a higher-priority URL already supplies the endpoint. Blank environment values are ignored. Non-Azure entries ignore these Azure variables.

Configure the built-in OpenAI provider and select a provider-qualified model:

```toml
[providers.openai]
auth = "api-key"
key_env = "AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY"
api_version = "2025-03-01-preview"

[providers.openai.deployments]
"gpt-5.4" = "my-gpt54-deployment"
```

With `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY` and either `AZURE_OPENAI_BASE_URL` or `AZURE_OPENAI_RESOURCE_NAME` in the environment, select `openai/gpt-5.4` (for example with `/model openai/gpt-5.4`). When neither `api_version` nor `AZURE_OPENAI_API_VERSION` is set, Responses defaults to `v1` and Chat to `2024-10-21`.

`dal.toml` strictly refuses supplied secrets. Setting keys such as `api_key`, `key`, or `secret` directly in configuration is rejected as an unknown key at load time. Credentials must come from environment variables named by `key_env` or through `dalgon login`.

Stored credentials live in `auth.json` under your product's data directory (`$XDG_DATA_HOME/dal/auth.json` or `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dalgona/auth.json`), written atomically with mode `0600` permissions (owner read and write only). Non-owner permission bits and symbolic links are refused. Stored entries record raw API keys, OAuth tokens, or structured envelopes; for example, GitHub Copilot stores a JSON envelope holding the token alongside any enterprise domain and discovered API endpoint.

Built-in providers resolve credentials from specific environment variables:
- `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`: GitHub token for GitHub Copilot (`github-copilot`) authentication.
- `GITLAB_TOKEN`: personal access token for GitLab Duo API key authentication.
- `GITLAB_CLIENT_ID`: overrides the default OAuth client ID for GitLab Duo.
- `GITLAB_REDIRECT_URI`: overrides the loopback redirect URI for GitLab Duo browser OAuth callback.
- `RADIUS_API_KEY`: API key for Radius (`radius`), sent as a bearer token.

Bedrock entries (`api = "bedrock"`) authenticate through captured AWS credential sources (environment variables such as `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, shared credentials and configuration files under `~/.aws/`, SSO tokens, external credential processes, or IAM roles) or a stored bearer token in `auth.json`. Provider readiness verifies credential availability against the effective configured provider family, including configured aliases, without performing network requests or writing to cache.

```toml
plugins = ["todo"]

[providers.custom]
api = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://api.example.com/v1"
key_env = "CUSTOM_API_KEY"
auth = "api-key"
```

## Write a minimal dal.toml

Set the defaults you would otherwise pass as flags on every run. A flag still wins for one run.

```toml
approval = "edits"
thinking = "high"
compact_ratio = 0.8

[serve]
port = 8080
```

This file approves edits without asking and still asks before `exec`. It raises the reasoning level, starts compaction at 80 percent of the context window, and moves the router to port 8080. Pick a model in the terminal, and dal saves `model` for you.

Add a plugin name to `plugins` only after its directory exists under `<data-root>/plugins/`. A plugin that fails to load stops startup. After you write the plugin from [Write a first plugin](plugins.md#write-a-first-plugin), add this line at the top of the file:

```toml
plugins = ["quality"]
```

Every config error names the key and the fix.

- [Rules](rules.md): set `rules.judge` and the other rule defaults.

## Before you start

A pi extension is TypeScript that pi loads with jiti. A dal plugin is Starlark that dal evaluates at load. Both run with your permissions. Neither is a sandbox. A port is a redesign more often than a translation. Read [Plugins](plugins.md) first. It defines every construct named below.

## Get the source

From npm, run `npm pack <package>`. It prints a file name. Then run `tar -xzf <file>.tgz`. It unpacks the file into `./package`. From git, run `git clone <url> package`. Pi's own examples are in `packages/coding-agent/examples/extensions/` of the pi repository.

## Take inventory

```sh
grep -RnoE '\b(pi|ctx)\.[A-Za-z_$][A-Za-z0-9_$]*' package --include='*.ts'
grep -RhoE "from '[^.][^']*'" package --include='*.ts' | sort -u
```

## See one tool ported

A pi tool of this shape:

```ts
pi.registerTool({
  name: "greet",
  description: "Greet someone by name.",
  parameters: Type.Object({ name: Type.String() }),
  async execute(id, params) {
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: `Hello, ${params.name}.` }] };
  },
});
```

becomes this plugin, saved as `greet/plugin.star`:

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def greet(ctx, args):
    return "Hello, " + args.name + "."

greet_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Greet someone by name.",
    input = dal.schema(name = dal.string()),
    run = greet,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "greet",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"greet": greet_tool},
)
```

The tool name moves from `name` to its key in `tools`. The schema moves from `parameters` to `input`. The result moves from a content list to the returned value.

## Map each call

| pi | dal | Shown in |
|---|---|---|
| `export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI)` | `plugin = dal.plugin(name = "...", version = "...")` in `plugin.star`, after one `load("@dal/v1", "dal")`; `name` matches the directory | every port |
| `pi.registerTool({name, description, parameters, execute})` | `dal.tool(description, input, run, uses)`, published as `tools = {"<name>": tool}`; `uses` lists the operations the handler may request | todo, subagent |
| TypeBox `Type.Object`, string enums | `dal.schema(...)` with `dal.string`, `dal.integer`, `dal.enum([...])`, `dal.list`; `dal.optional` for a field a caller may omit | todo, ask |
| `execute(id, params, signal, onUpdate, ctx)` | `run(ctx, args)`; dal cancels the call and discards the result; progress text is not ported | subagent |
| result `{content, details}` | the returned value; `dal.output(value = ..., view = ...)` when people should see a table or text apart from the data; `details` has no counterpart | todo (the returned value) |
| `throw` inside `execute` | `return dal.err(code, message)` for a failure the model should read; a failed operation stops the handler by itself | fetch |
| `renderCall`, `renderResult` | the result and its `view`; plugin UI is data | todo |
| `pi.registerCommand(name, {handler})` | `dal.command(tool = tool, positional = [...])` under `commands`; the command runs a tool and is typed as `/<plugin>:<key>` | todo, git-checkpoint |
| `ctx.ui.select`, `confirm`, `input` | `ctx.ask.select`, `ctx.ask.confirm`, `ctx.ask.text`, with the `ask.*` ids in `uses` | ask |
| `pi.exec(cmd, args, {cwd, timeout})` | `ctx.tools.exec("cmd args")` with `tools.exec` in `uses`; the approval ladder applies; a non-zero exit stops the handler unless you call `ctx.try_call(ctx.tools.exec, "...")`; `ctx.describe("tools.exec")` lists the other keywords | git-checkpoint |
| `fetch`, npm HTTP clients | `ctx.net.fetch(...)` with `net.fetch` in `uses` | fetch |
| `pi.sendUserMessage(text)` | `ctx.turn.steer(...)` with `turn.steer` in `uses`; `ctx.turn.wake` starts a turn when dal is idle | steer |
| state in `details`, `pi.appendEntry` | `ctx.state.read(key = ...)` and `ctx.state.write(key = ..., value = ..., expected = revision)`, with `state.read` and `state.write` in `uses` | todo, plan-mode, handoff |
| `before_agent_start` adds to `systemPrompt` | `prompt = "..."` on the plugin for fixed text; a `before_turn` hook that returns `event.append(text)` for per-turn text; the hook cannot read state | hello (`prompt`) |
| `pi.on("tool_call")` | `dal.on("tool_call", handler)`; the handler returns `event.allow()`, `event.block(reason)`, or `event.rewrite(args)` | permission-gate |
| other `pi.on` events | `dal.on` with `input`, `before_turn`, `before_request`, `tool_result`, `turn_end`, `session_start`, `session_end`, or `settled`; each event fixes its verdict methods and the operations it may request | none |
| `pi.on("user_bash")`, whole-operation swap | does not port; no hook can hand over execution | (not-port table) |
| `pi.registerProvider` | does not port; providers are dal core and aliases live in config | (not-port table) |
| `ctx.ui.custom`, widgets, status, editor | does not port; plugin UI is data | (not-port table) |
| `ctx.modelRegistry` nested model call | `ctx.models.infer` with `models.infer` in `uses`, or a child session through `ctx.agents.start` and `ctx.agents.wait` | subagent, handoff (child sessions) |
| `pi.registerFlag`, `registerShortcut` settings | `config = dal.schema(...)` on the plugin and a `[plugin.<name>]` table in `dal.toml`; the handler reads `ctx.config` | permission-gate, mcp |
| `pi.events` plugin bus | does not port; a handler cannot call another plugin's tool | (not-port table) |
| stdio MCP servers | `ctx.mcp.call` with `mcp.call` in `uses`, where a client is composed into the host; pure dal bundles none, so the call fails closed, and dalgona ships the MCP battery. An external bridge program covers the rest | mcp |
| project `.pi/extensions` | never loads; plugins come from the data root only | (not-port table) |
| TypeScript or npm at run time | an external program through `ctx.tools.exec`, or a port of the logic | (not-port table) |
| `resources_discover` dynamic skills | `skills = {"<name>": dal.skill(description = ..., path = "skills/<name>/SKILL.md")}`, fixed at load; no dynamic discovery | skill-pack |

## Decide

If the purpose of the extension is in the not-port table, do not port it.

| pi shape | why it does not port | what dal or dalgona offers instead |
|---|---|---|
| `interactive-shell` | needs user takeover of the terminal; `tools.exec` waits for the child to exit and captures its streams; `ask` is one modal question | none today; the door can widen |
| `status-line` | needs a persistent status or footer surface; plugin UI is data, and the only widget is `ask` | none today; the door can widen |
| `pi.on("user_bash")` swap | no hook can hand over execution | run the program as a tool through `ctx.tools.exec` |
| `pi.registerProvider` | providers are dal core | config aliases |
| `ctx.ui.custom`, widgets, status, editor | plugin UI is data | the ask surface |
| `pi.events` bus | a handler cannot call another plugin's tool | one plugin, or a file that both read |
| project `.pi/extensions` | plugins come from the data root only | install into the data root |
| TypeScript or npm at run time | nothing runs TypeScript at load | an external program through `ctx.tools.exec`, or a port of the logic |
| web fetch, MCP client as a product | dalgona's batteries own them | dalgona's `web` and `mcp` batteries; in dal the `net.fetch` operation |

## Create the plugin directory

```sh
d="${XDG_DATA_HOME:-$HOME/.local/share}/dal/plugins/<name>"; mkdir -p "$d"
```

On Windows the data root follows [Install dal and dalgona](install.md).

## Start from the nearest example

Pick the example that is nearest to your extension. For a tool with state, use `todo`. For child sessions, use `subagent`. For questions to the user, use `ask`. For an MCP call, use `mcp`. For a hook, use `permission-gate`. For skills only, use `skill-pack`. For the smallest shape, use `hello`. For an HTTP fetch, use `fetch`. For turn steering, use `steer`. For review rules, use `review-rules`. For file search and read, use `locate`. For session hooks with state, use `session-log`. For one environment variable, use `env-read`. The page `dal://examples/<name>` holds every file. From the repository root of a source checkout, run `cp -r examples/plugins/<name>/. "$d/"`. Then set `name` and rename the tools and commands.

## Translate

Translate one registration at a time with the map. The worked pair is pi `examples/extensions/todo.ts:105-297` beside the `todo` handler of `examples/plugins/todo/plugin.star`.

## Turn it on

Add the name to the plugins key in `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/dal/dal.toml`:

```toml
plugins = ["<name>"]
```

Run dal. A load error stops startup and names `path:line:col`. Then run one print-mode turn that uses the new tool, with the CLI print-mode flag.

## Change and reload

Edit the plugin. Then type `/reload`. Success prints counts, for example `Reloaded 2 plugins: 3 tools. New turns use them. A running turn keeps the plugins it started with.` Failure prints `reload failed: <rendered error>` on one line and `the previous plugin set stays live` on the next. With no plugins configured, it prints `No plugins to reload: the plugins key in dal.toml is empty.`

## Check it in dalgona

Copy the directory to the dalgona data root. Add the name to dalgona's config. Run `dalgona`. A plugin that loads in dalgon loads in dalgona.

## Write README.md

Write `README.md` in the plugin directory. Use these sections: `# <name>`, `Ported from`, `What it shows`, `What differs from pi`, `Install`, `Settings`. Use at most 60 lines. When you translate pi code, keep pi's MIT notice. `dal://examples` holds the text.

## Let dal port it

Type: `Port the pi extension in ./package to a dal plugin named <name>. Read dal://convert-pi and follow its steps. Write the plugin under the dal data directory, and tell me what did not port.` The model writes into the data root, so the approval ladder asks first. The `port-pi-extension` skill of `skill-pack` routes the model here.

## Next

- [Example plugins for dal](examples.md): copy the ported example nearest to your extension.
- [Plugins](plugins.md): look up each construct in the plugin reference.

    ("examples/ask", "# ask: Ask the user several questions in a row.

## Ported from
pi `questionnaire`

## What it shows
Questions to the user through `ask.select` and `ask.text`. The `questionnaire` tool takes 1 to 8 questions, each with an `id`, a `prompt`, and optional `options` (2 to 10 strings). A question with options is a choice list with one extra choice, "Type an answer". A question without options is a text prompt. The tool returns one `id: answer` line per question, and a blank answer reads `no answer`. The `ask` operations need to be declared in `uses` but need no grant.

Without a connected controller that can answer questions, each question returns
`no answer`. The tool does not wait for input or choose an option for you.

## What differs from pi
Each question is one modal prompt, asked in order. There is no form or custom screen. The schema accepts an `allow_other` field, but the handler does not read it.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `ask` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def questionnaire(ctx, args):
    lines = []
    for question in args.questions:
        qid = question.id
        prompt = question.prompt
        options = getattr(question, "options", dal.MISSING)
        if options == dal.MISSING:
            options = []
        if options:
            choices = [{"label": option} for option in options]
            choices.append({"label": "Type an answer"})
            answer = ctx.ask.select(prompt = prompt, options = choices, multi = False)
        else:
            answer = ctx.ask.text(prompt = prompt)
        if not answer:
            answer = "no answer"
        lines.append(qid + ": " + answer)
    return "\n".join(lines)

question = dal.schema(
    id = dal.string(),
    prompt = dal.string(),
    options = dal.optional(dal.list(dal.string(), min_len = 2, max_len = 10)),
    allow_other = dal.optional(dal.boolean()),
)

questionnaire_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Ask the user several questions in a row and return every answer. Use it when you need more than one decision before you continue.",
    input = dal.schema(questions = dal.list(question, min_len = 1, max_len = 8)),
    uses = ["ask.select", "ask.text"],
    run = questionnaire,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "ask",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"questionnaire": questionnaire_tool},
)
```

    ("examples/env-read", "# env-read: Read one environment variable.

## Ported from
Original to dal; no pi counterpart.

## What it shows
One tool over `env.read` and a plugin setting. The `read` tool takes a variable name, or falls back to the `key` setting from `[plugin.env-read]`. The host reads from the environment it captured at start. An unset variable returns an `env-read` error that names it. With no name and no `key` setting, the tool returns an error that says how to give one.

## What differs from pi
Pi reads `process.env` directly. Here the first read asks for the plugin's `env` grant, and the tool declares exactly one operation.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `env-read` to `plugins`.

## Settings
`key`: the default variable name when the tool gets none.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def read_env(ctx, args):
    name = args.name
    if not name:
        name = ctx.config.key
    if not name:
        return dal.err("env-read", "give a name, or set key in [plugin.env-read]")
    value = ctx.env.read(key = name)
    if value == None:
        return dal.err("env-read", name + " is not set")
    return value

read_env_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Read one environment variable. Give a name, or set a default key in [plugin.env-read].",
    input = dal.schema(name = dal.string(default = "")),
    uses = ["env.read"],
    run = read_env,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "env-read",
    version = "0.1.0",
    config = dal.schema(key = dal.string(default = "")),
    tools = {"read": read_env_tool},
    commands = {
        "env": dal.command(
            tool = read_env_tool,
            positional = ["name"],
            description = "Read an environment variable.",
        ),
    },
)
```

    ("examples/fetch", "# fetch: Fetch one URL over HTTP.

## Ported from
Original to dal; no pi counterpart. Pi reaches the network with `fetch` or an npm HTTP client.

## What it shows
The `net.fetch` operation and a failure the model can read. The `fetch` tool takes a `url`, sends an HTTP GET through `net.fetch`, and returns one line with the status and the body size. A transport failure returns a `fetch_failed` error naming the URL and the host message; a non-200 status returns a `fetch_failed` error naming the status. The command `/fetch:fetch` takes the URL as its positional argument.

## What differs from pi
Pi code awaits a response object and reads its body as text. This plugin reads `status` and the length of `body` from the host response record and never renders the body itself.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `fetch` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
"""Fetch one URL over HTTP and report its status and body size."""

load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def fetch_url(ctx, args):
    """Fetch one URL and return its status line.

    Args:
        ctx: Invocation context with the net service.
        args: Command arguments holding the url to fetch.

    Returns:
        One line with the status and body size, or a fetch_failed
        domain error when the request or the status fails.
    """
    result = ctx.try_call(ctx.net.fetch, method = "GET", url = args.url)
    if not result.ok:
        return dal.err("fetch_failed", "Could not fetch " + args.url + ": " + result.error.message)
    response = result.value
    if response.status != 200:
        return dal.err("fetch_failed", "GET " + args.url + " returned status " + str(response.status))
    return "GET " + args.url + ": status 200, " + str(len(response.body)) + " body bytes"

fetch_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Fetch one URL with an HTTP GET and report its status and body size.",
    input = dal.schema(url = dal.string()),
    uses = ["net.fetch"],
    run = fetch_url,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "fetch",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"fetch": fetch_tool},
    commands = {"fetch": dal.command(tool = fetch_tool, positional = ["url"], description = "Fetch one URL.")},
)
```

    ("examples/git-checkpoint", "# git-checkpoint: List and restore git stash checkpoints.

## Ported from
pi `git-checkpoint`

## What it shows
A tool and a command that run a program through `tools.exec`. The model tool `checkpoint` and the command `/git-checkpoint:checkpoint` accept `action` (`list` or `restore`, default `list`) and `n` (default `0`); the command takes them as positional arguments. `list` runs `git stash list` and prints the result, or `no checkpoints` when it is empty. `restore` runs `git stash apply stash@{n}`. Every git run passes the approval ladder. During a turn, dal asks before it runs. A slash command runs outside a turn, where no one can answer, so its git run fails closed with the approval message.

## What differs from pi
This plugin only lists and restores. It does not create checkpoints. The pi hook runs `git stash create` at each turn start and offers to apply that stash when you branch from the turn. A failed git command stops the handler with its error.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `git-checkpoint` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def checkpoint(ctx, args):
    if args.action == "restore":
        return ctx.tools.exec(command = "git stash apply stash@{" + str(args.n) + "}")
    result = ctx.tools.exec(command = "git stash list")
    if "stash@{" not in result:
        return "no checkpoints"
    return result

checkpoint_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "List or restore checkpoints.",
    input = dal.schema(
        action = dal.enum(["list", "restore"], default = "list"),
        n = dal.integer(min = 0, default = 0),
    ),
    uses = ["tools.exec"],
    run = checkpoint,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "git-checkpoint",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"checkpoint": checkpoint_tool},
    commands = {
        "checkpoint": dal.command(
            tool = checkpoint_tool,
            positional = ["action", "n"],
            description = "List checkpoints.",
        ),
    },
)
```

    ("examples/handoff", "# handoff: Distill the session into a handoff note.

## Ported from
pi `handoff`

## What it shows
Child sessions, saved state, and tool execution together. The command `/handoff:handoff` has no positional parameters. Pass `--note=...`, or give the model tool `handoff` its optional `note` argument. The child receives a prompt for the goal, state, next steps, and open questions. The child is unnamed, so the command can run again in the same workspace.

After the child finishes, the plugin saves its report under the session state key `handoff.md`. Success returns `Handoff written to handoff.md. Start the next session and ask for it.` In an ephemeral session, state is `unavailable`, so the command returns `handoff: no sidecar in an ephemeral session` and saves no note.

## What differs from pi
This plugin does not switch the parent session. It stores the note in the plugin's saved state. Child progress text is not shown. Cancelling a parent turn during `agents.wait` closes the awaited child and its descendants. Before the wait begins, cancel started children explicitly rather than relying on turn cancellation. Closing the parent session closes its descendant sessions.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `handoff` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def handoff(ctx, args):
    note = args.note
    started = ctx.agents.start(
        prompt = "Distill this session into a handoff note for a fresh session: current goal, state, next steps, open questions. " + note,
    )
    report = ctx.agents.wait(id = started.value.id)
    text = report.value.report.text
    state = ctx.try_call(ctx.state.read, key = "handoff.md")
    if not state.ok:
        if state.error.code == "unavailable":
            return "handoff: no sidecar in an ephemeral session"
        return state.unwrap()
    saved = ctx.try_call(
        ctx.state.write,
        key = "handoff.md",
        value = text,
        expected = state.value.revision,
    )
    if not saved.ok:
        if saved.error.code == "unavailable":
            return "handoff: no sidecar in an ephemeral session"
        return saved.unwrap()
    return "Handoff written to handoff.md. Start the next session and ask for it."

handoff_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Write a handoff note.",
    input = dal.schema(note = dal.string(default = "")),
    uses = ["agents.start", "agents.wait", "state.read", "state.write"],
    run = handoff,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "handoff",
    version = "0.1.0",
    commands = {"handoff": dal.command(tool = handoff_tool, description = "Write a handoff note.")},
)
```

    ("examples/hello", "# hello: The smallest dal plugin.

## Ported from
pi `hello`

## What it shows
One tool, one prompt section, and one skill in a single `plugin` value. The `hello` tool takes no arguments and returns a greeting. The prompt section tells the model to greet the user warmly. The `hello` skill points at `skills/hello/SKILL.md`.

## What differs from pi
Nothing to translate: pi's `hello` registers one tool, and so does this plugin. The prompt section and the skill are additions that show the other two kinds of registration.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `hello` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark

`servers_json` is optional text holding a JSON object with a `servers` map:

def mcp_settings(ctx):
    raw = getattr(ctx.config, "servers_json", dal.MISSING)
    if raw == dal.MISSING or not raw:
        return {"servers": {}, "timeout_ms": 30000}
    return json.decode(raw)

def mcp_list(ctx, args):
    servers = mcp_settings(ctx).get("servers", {})
    server = args.server

        info = servers.get(server, {})
        if not info:
            return ""
        response = ctx.mcp.call(server = server, tool = "", arguments = {})
        if getattr(response, "isError", False):
            return dal.err("mcp_error", response.text)
        if not response.text:
            return server + "  " + info.get("url", "")
        return server + "  " + info.get("url", "") + "\n" + response.text

A `tool_call` hook decides on its own: it can allow, block, or rewrite the call. It cannot ask you a question, because a deciding hook may request no operations. The match is a plain substring test, so it is a guard rail, not a security boundary.

def load_patterns(ctx):
    patterns = ["rm -rf", "sudo", "force"]
    extra = getattr(ctx.config, "patterns", dal.MISSING)
    if extra != dal.MISSING:

    ("examples/session-log", "# session-log: Remember sessions and turns in state.

## Ported from
Original to dal; no pi counterpart.

## What it shows
Two stateful hooks plus a reader. The `session_start` hook records `start` and the `turn_end` hook records `turn` in the `session-log.json` state key. Both hooks call through `ctx.try_call`, so an ephemeral session records nothing and raises nothing. The list keeps the newest 50 entries. The `log` tool and the `/session-log:log` command print one marker per line.

`session_start` runs before a client attaches, so no one can answer a grant question then. The first open of a session records no `start`. If you approve the plugin's state grant for good rather than for one session, later opens record `start`.

## What differs from pi
Pi keeps this kind of journal in extension memory. Here the hooks persist it in plugin state, so a reopened session reads what earlier turns wrote.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `session-log` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None. State needs a saved session; an ephemeral session records nothing.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def remember(ctx, mark):
    seen = ctx.try_call(ctx.state.read, key = "session-log.json")
    if not seen.ok:
        if seen.error.code == "unavailable":
            return None
        seen.unwrap()
    marks = []
    if seen.value.present:
        marks = [entry for entry in seen.value.value]
    marks.append(mark)
    if len(marks) > 50:
        marks = marks[len(marks) - 50:]
    saved = ctx.try_call(
        ctx.state.write,
        key = "session-log.json",
        value = marks,
        expected = seen.value.revision,
    )
    if not saved.ok:
        if saved.error.code == "unavailable":
            return None
        saved.unwrap()
    return None

def on_start(ctx, _event):
    remember(ctx, "start")
    return None

def on_turn_end(ctx, _event):
    remember(ctx, "turn")
    return None

def show_log(ctx, _args):
    record = ctx.state.read(key = "session-log.json")
    if not record.present:
        return "session-log: no turns recorded yet"
    lines = []
    for entry in record.value:
        lines.append("- " + entry)
    return "\n".join(lines)

log_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Show the session markers recorded by the session hooks.",
    input = dal.schema(),
    uses = ["state.read"],
    run = show_log,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "session-log",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"log": log_tool},
    commands = {"log": dal.command(tool = log_tool, description = "Show recorded session markers.")},
    hooks = [
        dal.on("session_start", on_start, uses = ["state.read", "state.write"]),
        dal.on("turn_end", on_turn_end, uses = ["state.read", "state.write"]),
    ],
)

    ("examples/subagent", "# subagent: Run tasks in separate dal child sessions.

## Ported from
pi `subagent`

## What it shows
Child sessions through `agents.start`, `agents.wait`, and `agents.cancel`. The `subagent` tool takes a single `task` string, or a `tasks` list of 1 to 8 items. If neither is provided, it returns `no task`.

Single-task execution:
1. Starts one child session with `agents.start`, passing the task as the prompt. The child runs in the same workspace with a fresh context.
2. Awaits the child with `agents.wait` to collect its final report.
3. Closes the completed child with `agents.cancel`.
4. Returns the report text. If the host refuses to start the child (for example, when maximum child depth is reached), the tool returns `subagent: child refused: <reason>`.

Multi-task batches:
The handler starts children in batches of up to 4 concurrent sessions, then awaits each one. `start_child` gives no session name, so the children are unnamed and concurrent starts do not conflict. If a start fails, the tool cancels the children it already started in that batch with `agents.cancel` and returns the start error.

## What differs from pi
The child receives only prompt text; its progress is not streamed back. A tool cannot call another plugin's tool, so delegation uses a child session. Cancelling a parent turn during `agents.wait` closes the awaited child and its descendants. Before the wait begins, cancel started children explicitly rather than relying on turn cancellation. Closing the parent session closes its descendant sessions.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `subagent` to `plugins`. Subagents are off by default in dal, so a session must allow them before the tool can start a child.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def cancel_children(ctx, handles):
    error = ""
    for handle in handles:
        result = ctx.try_call(ctx.agents.cancel, id = handle)
        if not result.ok and not error:
            error = "subagent: child cancel failed: " + result.error.message
    return error

def start_child(ctx, task):
    result = ctx.try_call(
        ctx.agents.start,
        prompt = task,
    )
    if not result.ok:
        return None, "subagent: child start failed: " + result.error.message
    started = result.value
    if started.type != "started":
        return None, "subagent: child refused: " + started.value.reason.type
    return started.value.id, ""

def wait_child(ctx, handle):
    result = ctx.try_call(ctx.agents.wait, id = handle)
    if not result.ok:
        return None, "subagent: child wait failed: " + result.error.message
    report = result.value
    if report.type != "await":
        return None, "subagent: child did not finish: " + report.type
    return report.value.report.text, ""

def run_batch(ctx, tasks):
    handles = []
    for task in tasks:
        handle, error = start_child(ctx, task)
        if error:
            cleanup_error = cancel_children(ctx, handles)
            if cleanup_error:
                return [], cleanup_error
            return [], error
        handles.append(handle)
    answers = []
    for handle in handles:
        answer, error = wait_child(ctx, handle)
        if error:
            cleanup_error = cancel_children(ctx, handles)
            if cleanup_error:
                return [], cleanup_error
            return [], error
        answers.append(answer)
        cleanup_error = cancel_children(ctx, [handle])
        if cleanup_error:
            cancel_children(ctx, handles)
            return [], cleanup_error
    return answers, ""

def subagent(ctx, args):
    tasks = getattr(args, "tasks", dal.MISSING)
    if tasks == dal.MISSING:
        tasks = []
    if not tasks:
        single = args.task
        if single:
            tasks = [single]
    if not tasks:
        return "no task"
    answers = []
    batch = []
    for task in tasks:
        batch.append(task)
        if len(batch) == 4:
            batch_answers, error = run_batch(ctx, batch)
            if error:
                return error
            for answer in batch_answers:
                answers.append(answer)
            batch = []
    if batch:
        batch_answers, error = run_batch(ctx, batch)
        if error:
            return error
        for answer in batch_answers:
            answers.append(answer)
    return "\n".join(answers)

subagent_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Run a task in a separate dal child session with a fresh context and return its final answer. Give one task, or up to 8 tasks that run 4 at a time. The child works in the same workspace.",
    input = dal.schema(
        task = dal.string(default = ""),
        tasks = dal.optional(dal.list(dal.string(), min_len = 1, max_len = 8)),
    ),
    uses = ["agents.start", "agents.wait", "agents.cancel"],
    run = subagent,
)

plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "subagent",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"subagent": subagent_tool},
)
```

    ("examples/todo", "# todo: Keep a todo list for this task.

## Ported from
pi `todo`

## What it shows
One tool with saved state. The `todo` tool takes an action (`list`, `add`, `toggle`, or `clear`), plus `text` for `add` and `id` for `toggle`:

- `list`: prints each item as `[ ] #<id>: <text>` or `[x] #<id>: <text>`, or `No todos` when the list is empty.
- `add`: requires non-empty `text`. Assigns an ID one greater than the highest existing ID and returns `Added todo #<id>: <text>`. Omitting `text` returns an error: `todo: text is required for add`.
- `toggle`: requires a nonzero `id`. Flips `done` and returns `Todo #<id> completed` or `Todo #<id> uncompleted`. Omitting `id` returns `todo: id is required for toggle`; an unknown ID returns `todo: #<id> not found`.
- `clear`: empties the list and returns `Cleared <n> todos`.

The list lives in session state under the key `todos`. Each write passes the revision from the read before it, so a stale write fails with a revision conflict instead of overwriting. The command `/todo:todos` prints the list.

## What differs from pi
pi keeps the list in the `details` of tool results and rebuilds it from the session. This plugin keeps it in saved state through `state.read` and `state.write`. In an ephemeral session, state operations fail closed as unavailable because no persistent store exists. There is no custom rendering: the tool returns plain text.

## Install
Copy to the dal plugins data root and add `todo` to `plugins`.

## Settings
None.

## Files

### plugin.star

```starlark
load("@dal/v1", "dal")

def todo_load(ctx):
    record = ctx.state.read(key = "todos")
    items = []
    if record.present:
        for item in record.value:
            items.append({"id": item.id, "text": item.text, "done": item.done})
    return items, record.revision

def todo_save(ctx, items, revision):
    ctx.state.write(key = "todos", value = items, expected = revision)

def todo(ctx, args):
    action = args.action
    if action == "list":
        items, _revision = todo_load(ctx)
        if not items:
            return "No todos"
        lines = []
        for item in items:
            mark = "x" if item["done"] else " "
            lines.append("[" + mark + "] #" + str(item["id"]) + ": " + item["text"])
        return "\n".join(lines)
    if action == "add":
        text = args.text
        if not text:
            return dal.err("todo", "text is required for add")
        items, revision = todo_load(ctx)
        new_id = 1
        for item in items:
            if item["id"] >= new_id:
                new_id = item["id"] + 1
        items.append({"id": new_id, "text": text, "done": False})
        todo_save(ctx, items, revision)
        return "Added todo #" + str(new_id) + ": " + text
    if action == "toggle":
        target = args.id
        if not target:
            return dal.err("todo", "id is required for toggle")
        items, revision = todo_load(ctx)
        for item in items:
            if item["id"] == target:
                item["done"] = not item["done"]
                todo_save(ctx, items, revision)
                if item["done"]:
                    return "Todo #" + str(target) + " completed"
                return "Todo #" + str(target) + " uncompleted"
        return dal.err("todo", "#" + str(target) + " not found")
    if action == "clear":
        items, revision = todo_load(ctx)
        count = len(items)
        todo_save(ctx, [], revision)
        return "Cleared " + str(count) + " todos"
    return "No todos"

todo_tool = dal.tool(
    description = "Keep a todo list for this task. Actions: list, add (text), toggle (id), clear.",
    input = dal.schema(
        action = dal.enum(["list", "add", "toggle", "clear"], default = "list"),
        text = dal.string(default = ""),
        id = dal.integer(default = 0),
    ),
    uses = ["state.read", "state.write"],
    run = todo,
)


plugin = dal.plugin(
    name = "todo",
    version = "0.1.0",
    tools = {"todo": todo_tool},
    commands = {"todos": dal.command(tool = todo_tool, description = "Print the todo list.")},
)
```

    ("guard", "# Complexity and anti-slop guard for agent edits

The guard checks every edit the model makes. It measures how much the turn grew the code and how complex the touched functions are. It also rejects an edit that leaves a file broken or half written. The guard is off by default in dal and on in dalgona.

Use it to catch two failures early. One is code that grows and gets harder to read each turn. The other is an edit that holds a placeholder instead of code. The guard blocks only invalid content. It reports everything else and leaves the decision to you.

## Turn it on or off

The `[guard]` table in `dal.toml` holds the switch. Turn the guard on in dal:

```toml
[guard]
enabled = true
```

Turn it off in dalgona:

```toml
[guard]
enabled = false
```

With the guard off, none of the reports and rejections on this page appear.

## Read a turn report

When a turn ends, the guard reports from its measurements of the files that turn touched. The report has four groups. The lines below show the shape of each group. Angle brackets stand for values.

**Turn growth.** The `TURN CHANGE SUMMARY.` line counts the lines the turn added and deleted, the net, and the files it touched.

```text
TURN CHANGE SUMMARY. Added <n>, deleted <n>, net <n>, files <n>, new files <n>. This is a report only; no automatic rewrite was started.
```

**Per-file absolute metrics.** Each patch call gives a receipt for each file it changed, up to 20 files. A receipt holds the code lines (`ploc`), the number of functions, and the sums of cognitive and cyclomatic complexity. Further files collapse into `guard: +<n> more files`.

```text
guard: <path> ploc <n> functions <n> cog-sum <n> cc-sum <n>
```

**Per-function metric changes.** A function that crosses a band gets one line with its metric before and after the turn. The metric is `cognitive`, `cyclomatic`, `ploc`, or `nesting`. A file that crosses the file-size band gets a `file` line. `new` stands for a function that did not exist before. The report ranks the crossings and keeps the ten largest.

```text
f <function> <metric> <before>→<after> (over <band>)
file <path> ploc <before>→<after> (over <band>)
```

**Best current.** A `METRICS:` line appears when a turn crosses a band, raises erosion, or churns a file. It gives the files touched, the bands crossed, and the erosion before and after the turn. Erosion is the share of complexity mass that sits in functions with a cyclomatic complexity above 10. A function's mass is its cyclomatic complexity times the square root of its code lines. When erosion rises by the report threshold, the line adds `(human baseline 0.34±0.22)`. Mass lines then rank the functions whose mass grew most. A path that the turn touched at least three times gets a `churn` line. Three is the default of `churn_turn_threshold`.

```text
METRICS: files <n>, bands crossed <n>, erosion <before>→<after>
f <function> mass <before>→<after>
churn <path> touched <n> times this turn
```

Every line names the file or the function and the metric. The report is text for you and for the model. It starts no rewrite.

## Know what the guard rejects

Two edits fail before they land. Each rejection leaves the file unchanged.

- A replacement that is mostly an omission placeholder, such as `// ... rest of the code` or `implementation omitted`, is rejected with `PATCH REJECTED. The replacement contains an omission placeholder. Write the complete replacement text; nothing changed.`
- An edit that leaves a parsed source file with a syntax error, or a `.json` file that does not parse, is rejected. The message reads `EDIT REJECTED. The file is not syntactically valid after this change. No change persists.` It then names the cause and the line. A file that already failed to parse before the edit is exempt.

Three notices only report. They name a fix and change nothing:

- `GUARD-WRAP NOTICE` flags a guard or fallback wrapped around unchanged code.
- `BROAD-HANDLER NOTICE` flags a new catch-all handler.
- `ABSTRACTION NOTICE` flags a new helper with one use.

The helper notice is off until you set `g4_enabled`.

A failed edit or command earns a strike. After three strikes on one repeated target, the guard blocks every further mutating call in that turn. These are edits, commands that write, and evals that act. Reads and pure evals still run. The message begins `Guard stopped this turn after 3 strikes.`

## Tune the thresholds

Set the thresholds under `[guard.policies]`. The bands live under `[guard.policies.bands]`.

```toml
[guard]
enabled = true

[guard.policies]
erosion_report_threshold = 0.1
churn_turn_threshold = 5

[guard.policies.bands]
cognitive = 20
function_ploc = 80
```

| key | default | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bands.cognitive` | 15 | the cognitive complexity band for one function |
| `bands.cyclomatic` | 15 | the cyclomatic complexity band for one function |
| `bands.function_ploc` | 50 | the code lines band for one function |
| `bands.nesting` | 4 | the nesting depth band for one function |
| `bands.file_ploc` | 500 | the code lines band for one file |
| `erosion_report_threshold` | 0.05 | the erosion rise that adds the mass lines |
| `churn_turn_threshold` | 3 | the touches per turn that add a `churn` line |
| `g4_enabled` | false | turns on the `ABSTRACTION NOTICE` |

An unknown key fails startup with `unknown guard policy key <key>`.

## Next

- [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) lists the `guard` key beside every other setting.
- [Tools, modes, and approval](tools.md) explains how `patch` and `exec` ask before they run.

    ("install", "# Install dal and dalgona from source (Linux, macOS, Windows)

Build dal and dalgona from source. Dal is the binary `dalgon`, with `dal` and `dl` as aliases. Dalgona is the binary `dalgona`, with `dg` as alias. After the build, run the [quickstart](quickstart.md) to sign in and run your first prompt.

No tagged release exists. No `dalgon-v*` or `dalgona-v*` tag has been created. The workspace version is `0.1.0`, but no tag exists for it. The registry and installer channels have nothing to fetch yet. When the first tags exist, those channels serve the same binaries.

## Build from source

You need git, the latest stable Rust toolchain, and a C toolchain. The symbol grammars compile through `cc`.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/gosuda/dalgona
cd dalgona
rustup update stable --no-self-update
cargo build --release --locked -p dalgon -p dalgona
export PATH="$PWD/target/release:$PATH"
```

In PowerShell, run the same first four commands. Then extend `PATH` with this line instead of `export`:

```powershell
$env:PATH = "$PWD\target\release;$env:PATH"
```

The binaries land in `target/release/`. The default Cargo target directory is assumed. `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` and `--target-dir` move it. The `PATH` line changes only the current shell. Add it to your shell profile to keep it. It puts `target/release` first, so these binaries win over another program named `dal`, `dl`, or `dalgon`.

Check the install:

```sh
dalgon --version
dalgona --version
```

`dalgon --version` prints `dalgon` and the package version. `dal` and `dl` print the same text. `dalgona --version` prints `dalgona` and the package version.

Source builds use the latest stable Rust toolchain. Run `rustup update stable --no-self-update` before building. The repository uses one root Cargo workspace and one `Cargo.lock`. It does not declare a minimum supported Rust version. Plugins need no toolchain.

## Platforms

Dal and dalgona build on Linux, macOS, and Windows on x86_64 and aarch64. The first prebuilt release binaries will arrive with the first tagged release. They will be unsigned in v0. Windows SmartScreen may warn about an unsigned binary. Verify the checksum where one is published before you run the binary.

## Config and data roots

Dal and dalgona use the same XDG-style layout on every OS. Only the way they find your home directory differs by OS.

| | dal (`dalgon`, `dal`, `dl`) | dalgona (`dalgona`, `dg`) |
|---|---|---|
| config file | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dal/dal.toml` | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/dalgona/dal.toml` |
| data root | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dal/` | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/dalgona/` |

Dal uses an `XDG_*` variable only when it is set to an absolute path. Otherwise it uses `.config` or `.local/share` under your home directory. A missing config file is valid. Dal then uses its defaults.

Your home directory comes from these variables:

| OS | Home directory |
|---|---|
| Linux and macOS | `HOME`, which must be an absolute path |
| Windows | The first absolute path of `HOME`, then `USERPROFILE`, then `HOMEDRIVE` joined with `HOMEPATH` |

If none applies, dal stops. On Linux and macOS it prints `dalgon: cannot find the home directory: HOME is not set`. On Windows it prints `dalgon: cannot find the home directory: none of HOME, USERPROFILE, or HOMEDRIVE+HOMEPATH is set`. Dal does not read `%APPDATA%` for config or data.

On Windows with `USERPROFILE` set to `C:\Users\alice` and no `HOME` or `XDG_*` variable, the paths are:

| item | path |
|---|---|
| config file | `C:\Users\alice\.config\dal\dal.toml` |
| data root | `C:\Users\alice\.local\share\dal` |
| plugin directory | `C:\Users\alice\.local\share\dal\plugins\<name>` |

Create a plugin directory in PowerShell under the same assumption:

```powershell
$d = Join-Path $env:USERPROFILE ".local\share\dal\plugins\quality"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force $d
```

Sign-in credentials live in `auth.json` in the data root. Dalgona has its own data root, so it has its own sign-in. [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) lists the keys of `dal.toml`.

## Next

- [Quickstart](quickstart.md) signs in and runs your first prompt.
- [Settings in dal.toml](config.md) lists every config key.
- [Plugins](plugins.md) shows how to write a plugin in the data root.

    ("integrate", "# Build a client on the dal protocol

A dal client talks to the agent over the dal protocol. Each message is one JSON object on one line. `dalgon` offers several ways in. This page builds a GUI client over `dalgon rpc`, then connects an editor and a Codex client.

Use the protocol to put your own UI, editor, or script in front of dal. The [protocol reference](protocol.md) lists every method.

## Choose a way in

| way in | command | frames |
|---|---|---|
| dal JSON-RPC on standard input and output | `dalgon rpc` | one JSON object per line |
| dal JSON-RPC on a local socket | `dalgon rpc --socket [FILE]` | one JSON object per line; `FILE` defaults to the per-user socket |
| Agent Client Protocol, for editors | `dalgon acp` | one JSON-RPC message per line |
| Codex app-server protocol | `dalgon app-server` | one message per line; frames omit `jsonrpc` |
| HTTP router, A2A, and WebSockets | `dalgon serve` | see [Run the dalgon model router and A2A server](serve.md) |

## Try it

Send one `initialize` request to `dalgon rpc`. The server ends when standard input ends.

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}' | dalgon rpc
```

The server answers with one line. Its `id` is `1`, and `result.protocolVersion` is `1`.

## Build a GUI client

Do these steps in order. Each request is one line on the standard input of `dalgon rpc`. Each reply is one line on its standard output.

1. Spawn `dalgon rpc`. Write one JSON object per line. Read one JSON object per line.
2. Send `initialize` first. List the capabilities you need. The result carries `protocolVersion`, the capabilities the server grants, and your `clientId`. Any other request before `initialize` fails with code `-32006` and `initialize must be the first request`. A second `initialize` fails with `-32600` and `initialize was already called`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":1,"clientInfo":{"name":"my-gui","version":"0.1.0"},"capabilities":["sessions","approval"]}}
   ```

3. Call `session/list` to show past sessions. `limit` runs from 1 to 500. A page that has more rows carries `nextCursor`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"session/list","params":{"limit":10}}
   ```

4. Call `session/open` to start or resume one. `workspace` must be an absolute path. The result carries `sessionId`, `gen`, and `view`. Other `ref` types are `resume` with `key` and `workspace`, `continue` with `workspace`, and `ephemeral` with `workspace`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"session/open","params":{"ref":{"type":"new","workspace":"/home/me/project"}}}
   ```

5. Call `session/subscribe` to receive updates. The reply holds `gen` and `seq`. Then the server sends `session/update` notifications. Each one names its update type in `params.update.type`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":4,"method":"session/subscribe","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>"}}
   ```

6. Call `session/submit` with a `prompt` command to start a turn.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":5,"method":"session/submit","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>","command":{"type":"prompt","expect":"idle","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Explain src/main.rs"}]}}}
   ```

7. Render updates as they arrive. A `request_opened` update asks you for an answer. Answer it once with `session/answer`. Use the request `id` as `requestId`. The `answer` is `{"type":"approve"}`, `{"type":"approve_for_session"}`, `{"type":"decline"}`, `{"type":"cancel"}`, or `{"type":"value","value":...}`.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":6,"method":"session/answer","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>","requestId":"<requestId>","answer":{"type":"approve"}}}
   ```

8. Cancel a running turn with `session/submit` and a `cancel` command. `turn` is the number of the running turn.

   ```json
   {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"session/submit","params":{"sessionId":"<sessionId>","command":{"type":"cancel","scope":{"type":"turn","turn":1}}}}
   ```

9. Read a stored blob with `blob/read`. Pass `sessionId` and `blobId`.
10. Reconnect with `session/subscribe`. Pass the `gen` you hold and `after`, the last `seq` you saw. A stale `gen` makes the server send a resync and resume at the head. An `after` beyond the head fails with `invalid params for session/subscribe: after <n> is beyond seq <m>`.
11. Generate your types from `protocol/schema`.

A wrong parameter fails with code `-32602`. The message reads `invalid params for <method>: <detail>`. A relative workspace fails with `invalid params for session/open: workspace must be an absolute path`.

## Client rules

- R1: answer each request exactly once.
- R2: never invent missing updates. Resync on gaps.
- R3: cancel cleanly. Do not abandon turns.
- R4: keep tokens secret. Never log them.
- R5: use one adapter for each transport. Never stack one adapter on another.
- R6: validate server replies tolerantly. Ignore unknown fields.

## Connect an editor over ACP

An editor that speaks the Agent Client Protocol starts `dalgon acp` as a child process. Register `dalgon acp` as the agent command in the editor settings. The command reads one JSON-RPC message per line on standard input. It writes one per line on standard output.

Check the command by hand:

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{}}' | dalgon acp
```

The reply carries `id` `1` and a `result`.

## Connect a Codex client

`dalgon app-server` serves the Codex app-server protocol. Its frames omit the `jsonrpc` member. A second `initialize` fails with code `-32600`.

```sh
printf '%s\n' '{"id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"clientInfo":{"name":"gate-client","title":"gate-client","version":"0.1.0"},"capabilities":{}}}' | dalgon app-server
```

The reply carries `id` `1` and a `result`.

## Next

- [Protocol](protocol.md) lists every method, capability, and error code.
- [Embed dal in a Rust program](sdk.md) shows the same agent as a Rust library.
- [Run the dalgon model router and A2A server](serve.md) serves the protocol over WebSockets.
